page_chunks.content:
## Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality

- Published November 15, 2026
- Views : 322
- 9 min read

Adventure riding asks a lot from your gear. It has to protect you when things go wrong, keep you comfortable when you're spending hours in the saddle, and be practical enough to live with when the ride takes you far from home.

The Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit is designed to do all three. It combines a touring jacket and pant with CE Level 2 D3O armour, abrasion-resistant materials, adjustable ventilation and a host of features aimed at making long-distance riding easier.

But a long list of features doesn't always tell you what a suit is like to use. So we put the Traverse through a series of simple tests and looked at it across three areas that matter most: comfort, mobility and protection, and touring practicality.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort

The first thing you notice about adventure riding gear is how much of it there is. You've got armour, reinforcements, multiple adjustment points and enough material to protect you when things don't go according to plan. The challenge is making all of this work without restricting your movement or becoming uncomfortable after a few hours.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## Mobility

We started with a simple question. How easy is it to move around in the Traverse?

We tried squatting, walking, climbing, getting on and off the motorcycle, and moving between seated and standing riding positions. These are all things you end up doing on an adventure ride, whether you're negotiating a difficult section of trail or simply stopping for a break.

The Traverse uses four-way stretch panels and multiple adjustment points to help with movement. These allow the jacket and pants to accommodate changes in riding position without making the suit feel unnecessarily restrictive.

The fit is particularly important around the shoulders, elbows, waist and knees. These are the areas that do most of the work when you're moving around on a motorcycle, and they need enough room to do so comfortably.

The idea here is simple. Riding gear shouldn't make it difficult to move around on the bike it's supposed to be used on.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## Ventilation

Heat is another thing you have to deal with when riding in India. A suit that works well on a cool morning can become uncomfortable once the temperature climbs, particularly when you're moving slowly or spending time in traffic.

The Traverse uses Reise's AirMorph ventilation system, which lets you adjust airflow through the jacket depending on the conditions.

We demonstrated this using a simple fan test, with lightweight ribbons around the ventilation openings to make the airflow visible. It's a basic way of showing how air moves around the suit when the vents are opened.

Of course, this isn't a test of how cool the jacket will feel on a hot afternoon. That depends on the temperature, humidity, riding speed and how much airflow actually reaches the rider. But it does help demonstrate the ventilation system and how it works.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
## Actual Comfort

Mobility and ventilation are important, but neither tells you the whole story.

The real question is how the suit feels when you're wearing it for an extended period. The weight of the gear, the fit around the shoulders and knees, the feel of the armour and how easily you can move around all contribute to the experience.

The Traverse is a substantial touring suit, so the expectation isn't that you'll forget you're wearing it. What matters is whether it allows you to get on with the ride without constantly adjusting the fit or feeling restricted.

The multiple adjustment points help tailor the fit, while the stretch panels allow for movement. The jacket and pants are also designed to work together rather than as two completely separate pieces of riding gear.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:
## Actual Comfort

Ultimately, comfort is something that becomes clearer with time in the saddle. A quick test can tell you whether the suit allows you to move, but longer rides are what tell you how well it works over an entire day.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 7)
page_chunks.content:
## Mobility & Protection

Protection is the main reason for wearing motorcycle gear in the first place. And with a suit like the Traverse, there's more to look at than just the armour inside it.

The protectors, outer materials, reinforcements, stitching and construction all play a part in how the suit is designed to perform.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## The Armour Test

The Traverse uses CE Level 2 D3O protection across several major impact zones.

The jacket gets D3O T5 EVO PRO X Level 2 shoulder and elbow protectors, along with a D3O Viper Air Level 2 back protector and D3O CP2 chest protectors. The pants use D3O T5 EVO PRO X Level 2 protectors at the knees and hips.

That's a fairly comprehensive spread of armour, covering the areas you'd expect to need protection in a fall.

For our test, we took a slightly less conventional approach. We dressed a host in the Traverse and put him through the Protection Detail Lab's very scientific Office Ambush Test, using plastic baseball bats to demonstrate the locations of the armour.

And before you try this at home, remember that we're willing to put our colleague in harm's way so you don't have to.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## The Armour Test

Jokes aside, this isn't a test of the armour's impact performance. That is what the CE certification is for. The demonstration simply gives us a way to show where the protectors sit and how the suit covers the major impact zones.

We also removed the D3O inserts to look at their shape, flexibility and construction. Flexibility matters because the armour needs to work alongside the movement of the rider rather than making the suit unnecessarily rigid.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Abrasion & Construction

Impact protection is only one part of the equation. The outer shell also needs to be able to deal with contact against rough surfaces.

The Traverse uses Cordura, SuperFabric reinforcement and heavy-duty ripstop construction across the jacket and pants. These materials are used to provide abrasion resistance and reinforcement in key areas.

To demonstrate this, we used rough surfaces such as concrete and gravel for a simple, controlled abrasion test. We then inspected the material and stitching up close.

This isn't a substitute for a standardised abrasion test, but it gives us a look at the materials and construction without simply reading out the specifications.

The reinforced panels are particularly worth looking at because not every part of a riding suit faces the same demands. Some areas need more reinforcement, while others need to allow for movement.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## Abrasion & Construction

The overall construction is designed to balance these requirements, rather than making the entire suit one thick, inflexible shell.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Water Resistance

Weather is another part of adventure riding that you can't always plan for. You could leave home in sunshine and find yourself riding through rain a few hours later.

The Traverse uses water-resistant construction designed to deal with changing weather conditions. To demonstrate how the suit handles exposure to water, we took it to a car washing centre and gave it a thorough soaking.

The test focused on the outer material, zips, closures and the connection between the jacket and pants. After the wash, we inspected the suit and checked the inside for signs of water ingress.

It's worth making a distinction here. A pressure wash is a useful visual demonstration, but it doesn't establish a formal waterproof rating or guarantee that the suit will keep you dry in every condition. The result also depends on how the garment is constructed, how the closures are secured and how long it's exposed to water.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Water Resistance

What this test does is give us a closer look at the suit's construction and how it responds to a direct and sustained spray of water.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Touring Practicality

Adventure riding gear has to do more than protect you on the motorcycle. You also have to live in it.

You put it on, ride for hours, stop for fuel, walk around, get back on the bike and repeat the process. The little details can make a difference over the course of a long trip.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Living In The Suit

The Traverse comes with several features aimed at making this easier.

The jacket has touring storage and adjustment options, while the pants get integrated suspenders. There's also boot compatibility, reflective detailing and a 360-degree zip that connects the jacket and pants.

The jacket-pant connection is particularly useful because it allows the two pieces to function as a complete touring system. It also means you're not relying on two completely separate garments to do their jobs.

The pockets and storage options are worth looking at in the same way. When you're touring, you want the things you need to be accessible without having to unpack your motorcycle every time you stop.

The suspenders help keep the pants in place, while the adjustment points let you fine-tune the fit. Reflective detailing adds another practical touch for riding in low-light conditions.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 16)
page_chunks.content:
## Living In The Suit

None of these features is particularly exciting on its own. But when you're wearing the suit for hours at a time, they're the sort of things you begin to appreciate.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 17)
page_chunks.content:
## Real-World Experience

This is where the lab tests take a back seat and actual riding becomes more important.

The suit might move well during a squat test, but how does it feel when you're standing on the pegs? The ventilation might work in front of a fan, but how useful is it once you're out on the road? And while the armour and reinforcements look reassuring, how comfortable are they after several hours in the saddle?

These are questions that are best answered by spending time in the gear.

Our real-world footage looks at the Traverse in use, from getting ready for a ride to spending time on the motorcycle and stopping along the way. It also gives us a chance to look at the suit as a complete system, rather than treating the jacket and pants as separate products.

The important things here are the fit, freedom of movement, ventilation, ease of use and how naturally the suit works with the rider's movements.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 18)
page_chunks.content:
## Real-World Experience

This is also where touring practicality comes into its own. The pockets, suspenders, adjustments and jacket-pant connection might not make much difference during a quick ride around town, but they become more relevant when you're spending an entire day in the gear.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 19)
page_chunks.content:
## The Verdict

The Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit brings together a comprehensive set of features for adventure and touring riders. The CE Level 2 D3O armour covers the major impact zones, while Cordura, SuperFabric and ripstop construction provide reinforcement across key areas. The four-way stretch panels, AirMorph ventilation system and multiple adjustment points address the demands of all-day riding, while the storage, suspenders, boot compatibility and 360-degree jacket-pant connection make it a more complete touring setup.

What matters, though, is how all these elements work together. Protection is important, but so is being able to move freely. Ventilation matters, but so does the fit. And a suit designed for long-distance riding needs to be practical enough to use day after day.

The Protection Detail Lab gives us a way to look at these features more closely, but the real measure of a touring suit is how well it works once you leave the studio and get out on the road.

page_chunks.title: Reise Traverse All-Terrain Suit Review | Comfort, Protection and Touring Practicality  - ZigWheels (part 20)
page_chunks.content:
## The Verdict

That's where the Reise Traverse ultimately needs to make its case.

TVS recently unveiled the RTR 125 at EICMA 2026. It is the brand’s most powerful 125cc bike, and is also one of the most hi-tech. The major highlight of the RTR 125 was unquestionably its striking and sharp design, and we think the brand should consider bringing the same design language to more motorcycles in its Indian lineup. While the newer design approach could make the Apache family look more modern and aggressive, several existing models are still carrying a silhouette that has remained largely unchanged for years.

The Apache RTR 160 2V, RTR 180 2V, RTR 160 4V and RTR 200 4V have received minor styling updates over the years. However, the basic design and overall silhouette have remained more or less the same. While these motorcycles still have their own identity, a more comprehensive design update would certainly make them look fresher and more appealing.

A well-executed update would not only attract new buyers but also be appreciated by enthusiasts who have followed the Apache range over the years.

After all, good styling can play a major role in a motorcycle’s appeal, especially in an increasingly competitive segment. A fresh design across the Apache lineup could give TVS a stronger visual identity while keeping its popular motorcycles relevant for years to come.

- Denza, the luxury sub-brand of BYD, enters India with 2 new EV models

Denza, the luxury arm of BYD, has set foot in India with two models, the D9 MPV and the Z9 GT. Both come as completely built unit (CBU) imports, with the D9 priced at Rs 90 lakh and the Z9 GT at Rs 1.56 Crore (ex-showroom). The D9 is for those who want a large, three-row electric MPV, while the Z9 GT is a, performance-focused 5-door EV that is the only shooting brake-type car on sale in India.

If you are wondering what this new brand brings to the table and want to know more about their new offerings, then read on as we cover both models in detail:

page_chunks.content:
## Exterior

The D9 boasts an upright face dominated by a large, blanked-off grille with vertical patterned elements. The grille is flanked by thick silver strips that merge into the LED DRLs, which sit below the dual-pod LED projector headlamps. The lower bumper gets a separate set of LED DRLs. The tall and flat-ish fascia is typical of a luxury MPV.

In profile, the D9 measures over 5.2 metres in length with a wheelbase of around 3.1 metres. It has a straight beltline and roofline, 18-inch dual-tone alloy wheels and powered sliding doors with a soft-close function.

The rear end features a chunky full-width LED tail-light bar, Denza lettering on the powered tailgate and a silver strip on the lower bumper that adds some contrast. It also gets a roof-mounted spoiler for a sporty look.

page_chunks.content:
## Interior

The D9 gets a seven-seat layout, featuring 2 seats at the front, two in the second row and three in the last row. The cabin gets Nappa leather upholstery, along with wood inserts and suede trims. To elevate the comfort, the second row gets individual captain seats with all the features that you would expect. Rear passengers have dedicated touchscreen controls in the armrests.

Similar to most BYD models, it gets a large 15.6-inch infotainment screen and plenty of storage spaces in the lower centre console. The flat bottom, two-spoke steering wheel further gives the interior a clean look.

The good thing is that all passengers get dedicated AC vents and grab handles.

Safety is taken care of by an ADAS suite, nine airbags, an electronic parking brake (EPB), a 360-degree camera with blind-spot monitor, front and rear parking sensors, ISOFIX child seat mounts, multiple parking sensors and a tyre-pressure monitoring system (TPMS).

## Exterior

The Z9 GT is unlike anything that you have seen in India. It comes in a unique new body style, featuring a sporty silhouette. At the front, the Z9 GT gets split LED headlamps with 108 lighting zones, a ridged bonnet and discreet air intakes on the bumper. A LiDAR sensor sits on the leading edge of the roof.

It measures around 5,180mm in length, 1,990mm in width and 1,490mm in height, with a 3,125mm wheelbase. It sits on 20-inch alloy wheels, a prominent character line, flush door handles for a premium effect, and the Denza logo on the D-pillars.

At the rear, you get a dual-ridge roof spoiler with a stop lamp in the centre, a heavily raked windscreen, wide LED tail-lamps and a layered bumper. A cool feature is that even the rear wheels steer by up to 15 degrees, which allows the Z9 GT to ‘crab walk’ and perform 360-degree turns.

The Z9 GT is a five-seater, and the dashboard is dominated by a triple-screen layout and a dual-tone cabin scheme. You also get a screen on each front door. On cars with camera-based mirrors, these show the camera feed, while on cars with conventional mirrors, they display a pattern synced with the ambient lighting.

The centre console gets multiple storage spaces for your mobile phones and cups, and there are also physical buttons for certain controls. It comes with a three-spoke steering wheel and well-bolstered seats.

Overall, the interior is a fun yet comfortable place to be in, with plenty of displays and a minimalist approach that looks clean.

The equipment list includes a triple-screen setup: a 17.3-inch central touchscreen, a 13.2-inch passenger screen and a 13.2-inch digital driver’s display. You also get powered seats with ventilation, heating and massage functions, an AR head-up display, four-zone climate control, connected car tech and a dual-pane sunroof.

Other features include a 20-speaker Devialet sound system, powered doors with soft-close, a powered tailgate and auto park assist.

## ZigSays...

Denza has picked two very different cars to introduce itself in India. Out of the D9 and Z9 GT, the former is the more practical of the two. It slots in as a plush, all-electric alternative to luxury MPVs like the Toyota Vellfire, and sits above the MG M9. The Z9 GT is the showpiece and the eye-candy. It is the only shooting brake on sale on our shores, with the BMW i7, Porsche Taycan and the Mercedes-Benz EQS as one of its closest rivals.

Both these cars will give BYD a distinct luxury offering in India that goes well beyond its existing lineup. Since Indians are moving towards luxury MPVs, there is a potential market for the D9 to capture. On the other hand, the Z9 could be a solid weekend car to have fun with, while also offering enough space inside to take your family for a joyride.

## Mahindra Scorpio-N Specs Decoded: The Numbers Behind Mahindra’s Toughest Family SUV

- Published November 11, 2026
- Views : 1415
- 13 min read

Say “Mahindra SUV” anywhere in India, and it brings to mind a name the nation trusts. For generations, families across the country have relied on Mahindra’s SUVs to take them wherever life leads, from mountain passes in the north to coastal highways in the south. Along the way, these SUVs have handled hill roads, village tracks and long highway journeys without missing a beat.

The Scorpio has been a big part of that story, and the Scorpio-N carries it forward. Its broad, upright body sits on a newly engineered ladder frame, and it gets two engines with real muscle. The 4x4 system has a proper low-range gearbox, and the suspension hardware is designed to make broken roads feel smoother. Put simply, it’s built the way a Mahindra SUV should be.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## Mahindra Scorpio-N Specs Decoded: The Numbers Behind Mahindra’s Toughest Family SUV

Spec sheets, though, rarely explain any of this in plain language. They’re full of kilowatts, rpm bands, linkages and acronyms that can sound like a foreign language. So we’ve gone through the Scorpio-N’s specs line by line and translated them. Here’s what each number means for you, from the frame up.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## The Foundation: A Frame Built From Scratch

Every tough SUV starts with what’s underneath, so that’s where we’ll begin. The Scorpio-N uses body-on-frame construction, built on Mahindra’s next-generation 3G frame. Mahindra says the frame was engineered from scratch rather than carried over, and it uses high-strength steel throughout.

**What it means:**

- **Body-on-frame** means the body sits on a separate steel chassis. It’s how trucks and serious off-roaders are built, with a stiff backbone that can take years of rough roads, heavy loads and trail abuse.
- **Monocoque**, used by most crossovers, combines the body and chassis into one shell. That works well in the city, but it isn’t designed for the same punishment.
- **High-strength steel** makes the structure stiffer and stronger without adding unnecessary bulk.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## The Foundation: A Frame Built From Scratch

**Why it matters to you:** That stiffness is what lets the Scorpio-N handle potholes, flooded roads and rocky trails year after year. It’s the base for everything else on this spec sheet.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
## The Engines: Mahindra Muscle, Two Ways

Mahindra SUVs have always been known for strong engines, and the Scorpio-N continues that. You get a choice of the 2-litre mStallion turbo-petrol or the 2.2-litre mHawk diesel. Both have the pull to move a full-size, three-row SUV with ease.

|  | **2-litre turbo-petrol (mStallion)** | **2.2-litre diesel (mHawk)** | **2.2-litre diesel (Z2/Z4 diesel MT)** |
| Fuel system | Turbocharged direct injection (TGDi) | Common rail direct injection | Common rail direct injection |
| Power | 203 PS @ 5000 rpm | 175 PS @ 3500 rpm | 132 PS @ 3750 rpm |
| Torque (MT) | 370 Nm @ 1750–3000 rpm | 370 Nm @ 1500–3000 rpm | 300 Nm @ 1600–2800 rpm |
| Torque (AT) | 380 Nm @ 1750–3000 rpm | 400 Nm @ 1750–2750 rpm | – |

**Decoding the numbers:**

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:
## The Engines: Mahindra Muscle, Two Ways

- **Power (PS):** Power determines how quickly you build speed and how easily you pass a slow-moving truck on the highway. The petrol’s 203 PS stays the same on every variant that offers it, from the base Z2 to the top Z8L.
- **Torque (Nm):** Torque is the pulling force you feel when you press the accelerator. In an SUV this size, it decides whether the drive feels relaxed or strained, especially with seven people on board and a full boot. The diesel automatic’s 400 Nm makes even a fully loaded Scorpio-N feel easy to drive.
- **The rpm band:** This tells you when the torque is available. On the diesel, the pull starts from 1500 rpm, which is the range you use every day in the city. You get strong acceleration without revving the engine hard.
- **Turbocharged direct injection (TGDi):** The turbocharger forces more air into the engine, and direct injection sprays fuel straight into each cylinder.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 7)
page_chunks.content:
## The Engines: Mahindra Muscle, Two Ways

Together, they let a 2-litre engine produce strong power for its size.
- **Common rail direct injection:** The diesel uses high-pressure fuel injection for strong pull and refined running. The engine also has an all-aluminium construction.

**Which one is for you?** Pick the petrol if you want strong acceleration and a refined, quiet character. Pick the diesel if you cover long highway distances, carry heavy loads or want to go off-road, since it’s the only engine offered with 4WD.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## The Gearboxes: Six Speeds, Cleanly Done

Both engines come with a 6-speed manual or a 6-speed torque converter automatic. Both gearboxes use a shift-by-cable setup.

**What it means:**

- **Shift-by-cable:** On older SUVs, a rigid metal rod linked the gear lever to the gearbox, so engine vibration came straight through into your hand. The Scorpio-N uses cables instead, which keeps the lever separate from the engine’s movement. Every shift feels cleaner, and the lever stays calm at idle.
- **Torque converter automatic:** This is a conventional automatic that is smooth in traffic and suited to an SUV’s heavy-duty work. It also gets a torque boost on both engines: 400 Nm on the diesel and 380 Nm on the petrol.

**Choose your mood:** Diesel versions get three drive modes.

- **Zip:** Soft and easy-going, for stop-and-go traffic.
- **Zap:** The balanced everyday setting.
- **Zoom:** Sharper throttle response for when you want a more engaging drive.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## RWD And 4WD: The Proper SUV Layout

Like a true Mahindra SUV, the Scorpio-N is rear-wheel drive. Diesel buyers can also choose four-wheel drive, which is where the Scorpio-N really sets itself apart from the crossovers it’s often compared with.

**What it means:**

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## RWD And 4WD: The Proper SUV Layout

- **Rear-wheel drive (RWD):** The rear wheels push the SUV forward, while the front wheels only have to steer. This layout is built for heavy loads, and it’s how tough SUVs and pickups have been made for decades.
- **Shift-on-the-fly 4WD:** You can switch from 2WD to 4WD while driving, without stopping or getting out. So when the road turns muddy, you just turn a dial and keep going.
- **4-High:** For slippery surfaces at normal speeds, such as wet grass, gravel, light snow or a sandy beach road.
- **4-Low:** A dedicated low gear range for the toughest terrain, like steep climbs, deep mud and rocky trails. It multiplies the engine’s torque, so the Scorpio-N can crawl slowly and steadily over obstacles with plenty of pulling force.

**Where to find it:** 4WD is offered on the Z4 diesel MT, the Z8T diesel (MT and AT) and the Z8L 7-seater diesel (MT and AT). A Scorpio-N 4x4 starts from Rs 18.03 lakh (ex-showroom).

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## 4XPLOR And BLD: Your Off-Road Assistants

Here’s the good news for first-time off-roaders: the Scorpio-N 4x4 doesn’t need an expert behind the wheel. Two smart systems take care of most of the hard work.

- **4XPLOR terrain modes:** Turn a dial to choose Normal, Snow, Mud & Ruts or Sand. The Scorpio-N then adjusts how it delivers power and manages wheelspin for that surface. You pick where you’re going, and it works out how to get there.
- **Brake Locking Differential (BLD):** Off-road, a common way to get stuck is when one wheel loses grip, either hanging in the air or spinning in mud. Most of the engine’s power then goes to that free wheel. BLD automatically brakes the spinning wheel, which sends power back to the wheels that still have traction.
- **Adventure Statistics:** The 4WD variants also show useful off-road information in the cabin, so you can see what the SUV is doing on the trail.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Climb And Descend With Confidence

Hills and steep slopes are where many drivers feel nervous, and where Mahindra SUVs have always been at home. Every Scorpio-N, from the Z2 up, comes with two features to help on slopes.

- **Hill Hold Control:** When you stop on an uphill slope, it holds the brakes for a moment as you move your foot to the accelerator. The SUV won’t roll back.
- **Hill Descent Control:** On steep downhill slopes, it automatically limits the SUV’s speed, so you can focus on steering instead of braking.

Both are standard on every variant, which makes the Scorpio-N comfortable on ghat roads and trails, whichever variant you buy.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Suspension: Where The Comfort Comes From

The suspension section is usually where a spec sheet loses most readers, but it’s also the secret behind the Scorpio-N’s ride. Here’s what’s under there, and what each part does.

| **Front** | **Rear** |
| Double wishbone with coil-over shocks, FDD and MTV-CL | Pentalink with Watt’s linkage, FDD and MTV-CL |

**Decoding the hardware:**

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Suspension: Where The Comfort Comes From

- **Double wishbone (front):** Each front wheel is held in place by two arms, one above the other. This keeps the tyre flat against the road as the suspension moves, so you get better grip and more precise steering on bumpy roads.
- **Coil-over shocks:** The spring and shock absorber are combined into one compact unit.
- **Pentalink (rear):** Five links hold the rear axle in place, which controls its movement more precisely than simpler designs. On broken roads, the rear stays more stable and composed.
- **Watt’s linkage:** An extra linkage that stops the rear axle from shifting sideways as it moves up and down. You feel it as a steadier rear end through corners and over uneven surfaces.
- **Frequency Dependent Damping (FDD):** This is clever shock absorber tech. FDD reacts differently to small, quick bumps, such as expansion joints and rough patches, than to big, slow movements like potholes and speed breakers.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Suspension: Where The Comfort Comes From

The small stuff feels softer, while the big hits are kept under control.
- **MTV-CL:** Valve technology inside the shock absorbers that works with FDD to fine-tune the ride quality.

**The result:** A body-on-frame SUV that handles bad roads better than many expect. Speed breakers, potholes and rocky tracks are absorbed in a controlled, composed way.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 16)
page_chunks.content:
## Steering And Brakes: Control You Can Feel

Strong engines need strong control, and the Scorpio-N is well sorted on that front.

- **Electric power steering:** Most versions get electric power steering. It’s light for parking and tight city lanes, and it becomes more precise at higher speeds.
- **Ventilated disc brakes on all four wheels:** Every Scorpio-N gets these, from the Z2 to the Z8L. The discs have internal air channels that help them cool quickly, so braking stays strong and consistent. That matters most on long downhill ghat roads, where brakes are used repeatedly.
- **ABS with EBD:** Standard across the range. ABS stops the wheels from locking under hard braking, so you can still steer. EBD balances braking force between the front and rear wheels depending on the load.
- **Electronic Stability Control (ESC):** Also standard. Mahindra’s ESC suite includes 18 functions that help keep the Scorpio-N stable during sudden manoeuvres, sharp turns and emergency braking.

page_chunks.content:

- **Width (1917 mm):** More width means more shoulder room across each row of seats.
- **Height (1857 mm):** You sit high above traffic, with a clear view of the road ahead.

page_chunks.content:
## Seating: Six Or Seven, Your Choice

A Mahindra SUV has always been built to carry the whole family, and the Scorpio-N gives you two ways to do it.

- **7-seater:** Standard across the range, with a bench in the second row. The third row folds and tumbles when you need more luggage space.
- **6-seater:** Offered on the top Z8L. It replaces the second-row bench with captain seats, so the middle-row passengers get more comfort and easier access to the third row.
- **6-way powered driver seat:** On the Z8T and Z8L, adjusting your driving position is done at the press of a button.
- **Ventilated front seats:** Also on the Z8T and Z8L, they keep you cool through hot Indian summers.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 20)

## Wheels And Tyres: Grip Meets Style

Tyre sizes can look like a random string of numbers, but each part tells you something useful. Here’s what the Scorpio-N gets:

- **255** is the tyre’s width in millimetres. Wider tyres put more rubber on the road for better grip.
- **60** is the sidewall height as a percentage of the width. Taller sidewalls cushion you over bad roads and off-road trails.
- **R18** means the tyre fits an 18-inch wheel.
- The Z8T and Z8L also get a tyre pressure monitoring system (TPMS), which shows the pressure and temperature of each tyre and alerts you if something isn’t right.

## ZigSays…

Some SUVs are made to look good outside a café. The Scorpio-N is made for the moments that test a car. It’s the overnight drive to your hometown, the monsoon week when the roads go underwater, and the detour that turns into a dirt track. It’s also the family trip where everyone’s luggage and everyone’s opinions have to fit in one vehicle. Its spec sheet reads like a list of answers to those situations.

What we like most is how naturally the Scorpio-N fits into everyday life. It doesn’t ask you to choose between a family car and an adventure vehicle, or between modern comfort and the confidence of tough hardware. It’s the same SUV on Monday’s office run and Saturday’s trail, and it doesn’t feel out of place in either. Very few vehicles can say that so convincingly.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Specifications Explained In Simple Terms  - ZigWheels (part 24)
page_chunks.content:

There’s also something reassuring about the badge. Mahindra has spent decades building SUVs for Indian roads, and the Scorpio-N carries all of that experience. You can sense it in how the SUV is put together: it’s been thought through for real conditions. That kind of reliability is hard to put a number on, but you notice it the first time a bad road doesn’t slow you down.

If you’ve been looking for one SUV that can do it all, the Scorpio-N belongs at the top of your list. Take it on your own roads, the ones you drive every day and the ones you’ve been meaning to explore. That’s where you’ll see why so many Indian families keep coming back to it.

## TVS Ntorq 150: Long Term Report 2,500km Part 2: Riding In Monsoons & Touring

- Published August 2, 2026
- Views : 4402
- 3 min read

The TVS Ntorq 150 has been with me for over 2 months now, and it’s become my daily rider. In the previous report, I said it’s a cheat code scooter since it’s as fun and as quick as some of the 150cc bikes. Since then, I’ve done a couple of long rides, including a Pune-Mumbai-Pune weekend run. And the recent cloudburst in Pune gave me a chance to experience how it performs when it gets super wet – I am ofcourse talking about the roads here.

page_chunks.title: TVS Ntorq 150: Long Term Report 2,500km Part 2: Riding In Monsoons & Touring  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## Riding In The Rain

I am going to start with this bit since I love riding in the rain. And, long story short, the Ntorq did not disappoint. Be it commuting to the office or a weekend vadapav ride in the rain, it was a ton of fun. The scooter holds its composure on wet roads as long as you don’t ride like an idiot. Never did it make me feel like I should wait in the shade till the rain subsided, for lack of grip or because it felt scary. The only reason I considered stopping was heavy downpour with very low visibility.

And unlike on a bike, I could either dump my bag in the boot or keep it on the floorboard, depending on how heavily it was raining, to keep it dry. +1 point for convenience.

page_chunks.title: TVS Ntorq 150: Long Term Report 2,500km Part 2: Riding In Monsoons & Touring  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## Long-Distance Riding

With great power comes great responsibility, and the ease of touring. While most scooters are discredited for touring because they can’t keep at highway speeds for long, the Ntorq 150 does it effortlessly. While riding down to Mumbai, and back, never did it feel out of breath or out of place. It can stay at highway speeds for extended periods. In fact, riding on the common patch of the Mumbai-Pune expressway did not feel unnerving at all. Only the bumpy surface prevented me from riding even faster.

While the seat is spacious enough for one, I felt a slight discomfort set in after two hours of saddle time.I considered taking a breather but Google Maps said I was not too far from home. So I decided to push on. Had I been on a longer ride, I would have definitely taken a break.

And not taking that break proved helpful since it increased my tolerance level a bit. The next day I rode the same distance back to Pune, without any noticeable discomfort.

page_chunks.title: TVS Ntorq 150: Long Term Report 2,500km Part 2: Riding In Monsoons & Touring  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## The Farewell

It’s time to bid farewell to Ntorq draws near. It’s that scooter, or in fact, a two-wheeler, that I will never mind swinging a leg over – irrespective of where I need to go, or what I need to do. While it keeps me away from my Duke, it ensures I have as much fun. Maybe I should check with my wife if her current scoot needs an upgrade, because I know the right one.

--

page_chunks.content:
## TVS Ntorq 150 Long Term Introduction: The Cheat-code Scooter

- Published June 15, 2026
- Views : 5203
- 3 min read

Back when the TVS Ntorq 150 had first arrived at our office last year, just a short spin on it made me keen on using the scooter for a longer duration. Fast forward to a month ago and now it is back for a long term test. And after badgering Jehan a lot, I ended up with its keys.

Also, I had been toying around with the idea of getting a scooter for myself, as a secondary ride. As much as I am happy riding my KTM 390 Duke, I felt a need for a “workhorse”. The Ntorq couldn’t have come in at a better time. Since then, I’ve covered almost 1000km including my everyday commutes, and some short rides.

page_chunks.title: TVS Ntorq 150 Long Term 900km Introduction Report  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## Scooter Comfort

Riding the Ntorq to office everyday was a welcome change. While my Duke wants to go all out all the time (not that I am complaining), I can either ride the Ntorq at a chill pace, or I can whack open the throttle for a dose of adrenaline.

And that, while being more frugal. I don’t need to worry about mileage, which the KTM has me thinking about sometimes in the wake of increasing fuel prices. At about 40kmpl, it’s almost twice that of my bike. However, the smaller fuel tank means I am visiting the petrol pump a similar amount. So, in all a win for the Ntorq.

And it also feels so roomy and spacious as compared to the bike. The result? My wife’s happier because now I don’t complain about getting groceries while coming back home.

page_chunks.title: TVS Ntorq 150 Long Term 900km Introduction Report  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## The Fun

While I haven’t yet had the time to go for long weekend rides, I did some short rides around Pune. I was surprised that the Ntorq could keep up with some bigger bikes on narrow, winding roads. It never felt lacking or slow. Hence, why I am terming it the cheat-code scooter. If you must get a scooter instead of a bike, this is what you need to check out. I had as much fun in those short rides, as I would have had on my Duke. And I was slightly more comfortable as well.

page_chunks.title: TVS Ntorq 150 Long Term 900km Introduction Report  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## Not Family Friendly

Every coin has two sides. As much fun as the Ntorq is, it’s not a family scooter. While I don’t mind riding alone on it, my wife doesn’t prefer to sit behind me *(Are you sure it isn’t just your riding? – Jehan)* since the seat is rather compact. She did take it out for a short spin in our complex and found it as much fun to ride it than sitting pillion, though.

page_chunks.title: TVS Ntorq 150 Long Term 900km Introduction Report  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
## A Keeper

I enjoy riding the Ntorq so much that now I want to see how fun and comfortable it is on the longer runs. I want to see if I can do my monthly Pune-Mumbai-Pune runs with it. Not that I doubt that it can, but if it can keep up the fun quotient, or if it fades and discomfort creeps in. Also, I am very keen on seeing if it can do it in one tank, considering its lower range. But at the end of the first one, I am a happy scooter boy.

Fuel Efficiency Achieved: 40kmpl

Positives: Comfort, Performance

Negatives: Compact seat

Touring On The Royal Enfield Himalayan 450: 5 Things I Learnt

- Dec 19, 2024
- Views : 3169

Getting your first long-term motorcycle always feels like a bit of a milestone. It’s not just about having a machine to get around anymore, it’s about building a connection, understanding its quirks, and slowly letting it become a part of your everyday life. For me, that moment came with the Hero Xpulse 210. It’s been about 1000km now, and while that’s still early days in the grand scheme of things, it’s been long enough to form some honest, initial impressions, not as a reviewer, but simply as a rider living with the bike.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xpulse 210 Long Term 1,000km Review: Fleet Introduction  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content: The first thing that stood out to me was how familiar yet different it felt. Having spent time around the older Hero Xpulse 200 4V, I expected the 210 to feel like a natural extension, and in many ways, it does. The core character is still very much intact. It’s approachable, unintimidating, and easy to get along with right from the get-go. But there’s also a noticeable shift in how it presents itself. The riding stance feels more accommodating now, slightly more relaxed yet purposeful, giving it a stronger “proper adventure bike” vibe. It’s the kind of posture that makes you want to keep riding, even when you don’t really have a destination.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xpulse 210 Long Term 1,000km Review: Fleet Introduction  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content: What really surprised me, though, was how seamlessly it slipped into my daily routine, especially when compared to my personal bike, the Bajaj Dominar 400. As my only bike, the Dominar 400 has been my go-to option for every type of riding, but in a city like Pune, it can sometimes feel cumbersome. The Xpulse 210, on the other hand, feels perfectly at home here. It’s lighter on its feet, easier to manoeuvre, and far less demanding in stop-go traffic. Suddenly, squeezing through tight gaps or making quick direction changes doesn’t feel like a task, it just happens naturally.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xpulse 210 Long Term 1,000km Review: Fleet Introduction  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content: And then there’s the roads, or rather, the lack of good ones. If you’ve spent enough time riding in Pune, you’d know that unpredictability is part of the experience. Broken patches, potholes, uneven surfaces, they’re all just part of the daily commute. But with the Xpulse 210, that constant sense of caution has faded away. I no longer find myself scanning every inch of the road or slowing down excessively for rough sections. The bike simply takes it all in stride. There’s a sense of reassurance in the way it absorbs bad roads, almost encouraging you to be a little less worried and a bit more spontaneous with your riding.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xpulse 210 Long Term 1,000km Review: Fleet Introduction  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content: The engine, at least for now, feels engaging enough for what I expect from this kind of motorcycle. It’s not about outright speed or aggressive performance, but more about how usable and responsive it feels in real-world conditions. There’s a certain liveliness to it that keeps things interesting, whether you’re cruising through traffic or just heading out for a short spin. Adding to that is the exhaust note, which has a surprisingly fun braap tone. It’s not overly loud or attention-seeking, but it has enough personality to make you enjoy those small bursts of acceleration.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xpulse 210 Long Term 1,000km Review: Fleet Introduction  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content: Of course, the experience hasn’t been completely flawless, but interestingly, the issues I’ve faced haven’t really been with the bike itself. I received the motorcycle with a broken rear-view mirror (courtesy of Jehan's small spill during a shoot). What made it more frustrating was the struggle that followed. Despite visiting multiple service centres around Pune, getting a replacement hasn’t been as straightforward as it should have been. It’s one of those things that doesn’t affect how the bike rides, but it does leave a bit of a dent in the overall experience.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xpulse 210 Long Term 1,000km Review: Fleet Introduction  - ZigWheels (part 7)
page_chunks.content:
That said, these are still early days, and the bigger picture remains quite positive. The Hero Xpulse 210 has already started to change the way I approach riding, making it less about avoiding bad roads and more about embracing them. And that, in a way, feels like the whole point of a bike like this. Looking ahead, I’m especially excited about what this motorcycle could help me explore next. More than just daily commutes or city runs, I now find myself thinking about trails, dirt paths, and the idea of actually improving my off-road skills, and for that, the Xpulse 210 feels like the perfect companion to grow with.

**Distance Covered Till Date:** 3630km

**Positives:** Comfort, Performance, Mileage

**Negatives:** Unavailability of spare parts

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex First Ride Review: Performance, Ride Quality, Handling, Features & More  - ZigWheels (part 1)
page_chunks.content:
Ceat SportRad Tyres 5,000km Review, on KTM 390 Duke

- Oct 6, 2024
- Views : 3320

When Royal Enfield first launched the Guerrilla 450 back in 2024, it was an interesting mix. On one hand, it felt familiar, thanks to the same Sherpa 450 engine we’ve seen on the Himalayan. But on the other hand, it felt completely unlike a typical Royal Enfield, especially with its aggressive power delivery and surprisingly agile handling.

It was exciting, no doubt. But it wasn’t perfect. There were a few niggles that made you pause… and think twice before putting your money down. Now, with the Apex variant, Royal Enfield claims to have fine-tuned the experience.

But has the brand actually fixed what held the Guerrilla back? Or is this just a minor update dressed up as something more?

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex First Ride Review: Performance, Ride Quality, Handling, Features & More  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
At first glance, the Guerrilla Apex doesn’t look drastically different, and that’s not a bad thing! It was already a good-looking motorcycle. There’s a new headlight cowl and a removable pillion seat cowl (for which you don’t get the right-sized tool in the factory-provided tool kit. Why Royal Enfield?), and three new colours (Apex Red, Apex Black and Apex Green). The red is definitely my pick of the lot as it looks absolutely rad. It accentuates the bike’s streetfighter stance, with a hint of that Ducati Monster vibe going on, which it really works.

Small updates, yes. But they add that extra bit of attitude the bike needed.

The new aluminium handlebar is slightly lower and a bit farther away. That’s it. Everything else, the seat and footpegs, stays the same.

But somehow, this small tweak changes how the bike feels in the twisties. You sit a little more forward, a little more engaged. Not uncomfortable… just more involved. And that sets the tone for what comes next.

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex First Ride Review: Performance, Ride Quality, Handling, Features & More  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
Because once you start riding it with that slightly sportier posture, you naturally begin loading the front wheel more. And that does two things: It improves front-end grip, and it boosts your confidence while cornering.

The Guerrilla already handled well earlier. But now? It just feels sharper. More connected.

Then came the new Vredestein Centuro ST tyres. Whether it was on a go-kart track or those twisty roads from Guwahati to Shillong, they just give you that extra confidence to push a little harder.

Even when things feel like they might go slightly off… they sort of reassure you like, “Relax, we’ve got this.” In fact, you’ll run out of cornering clearance before you run out of grip. The tyres also play a big role under hard braking. They help the bike maintain its composure and continue to inspire confidence even when you grab a handful of the lever.

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex First Ride Review: Performance, Ride Quality, Handling, Features & More  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
Now, the roads we rode on were honestly some of the best ghats in the country, and the go-kart track was butter-smooth. So ride quality isn’t something we could test thoroughly. That said, the rear suspension remains unchanged, and that shows. On smooth roads, it does its job well, keeping the bike planted and the ride comfortable. But hit a small rough patch, and you’ll have to slow down considerably. Because if you don’t, the bike does feel like it wants to throw you off the seat.

So yes, while the handling has improved, the ride quality still has that slightly firm, sporty edge to it.

The 452cc single-cylinder, liquid-cooled Sherpa engine was always the highlight. It still makes the same amount of power and torque (40PS and 40Nm). Punchy, torquey, and fun, and that hasn’t changed. What has changed, though, is how usable it feels.

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex First Ride Review: Performance, Ride Quality, Handling, Features & More  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
Earlier, the riding modes didn’t really feel all that different. Even the calmer mode felt a bit jumpy. Now, with City and Sport modes, replacing the earlier Eco and Performance, there’s a clear distinction. City mode is smoother, calmer, and easier to live across the rev range. Switch to Sport, and that lively, slightly aggressive character comes back.

It finally feels like the modes actually do something.

Feature-wise, things remain mostly the same, but with a couple of genuinely useful additions. The biggest one? You can now use Google Maps navigation even with the screen switched off. It’s currently limited to Android, but still super handy. You also get GPX route support and ride data sharing, which adds to the overall riding experience. That said, your phone battery will still take a hit, so keep that charger handy.

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex First Ride Review: Performance, Ride Quality, Handling, Features & More  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:
Here’s the thing. The Guerrilla 450 was always a fun motorcycle. It had character, it handled well… but it also had a few rough edges. With the Apex, those edges feel smoother. The bike feels more confident. More sorted. More complete.

At Rs 2,49,999 (ex-showroom) for the base Apex Red, it shows what happens when Royal Enfield leans a bit more towards being sporty. Sure, a quickshifter and traction control would’ve made it even more exciting. But even then, this just feels almost complete. Would this mid-life update be better with a tweak to the suspension settings? Definitely. Does it make it less fun, though? Not at all.

Touring On The Royal Enfield Himalayan 450: 5 Things I Learnt

- Dec 19, 2024
- Views : 3169

Three months and close to 3,000km later, the Eurogrip Trailhound SCR tyres on my KTM 390 Adventure X have now been tested primarily in city traffic and on highways. With the initial impressions well behind me, here’s how they’ve performed in everyday road-focused usage.

On tarmac, while the **initial impressions were quite good**, the Trailhound SCRs offer decent grip levels. That said, grip is still more than adequate for daily riding and touring, although the stock tyre set felt a bit grippier. During cornering, the tyres hold their line well and feel predictable, even when leaned over at speed.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip Trailhound SCR Long-Term Review: 3 Months & 3,000km Done  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
Thanks to their rounder profile, when compared to the stock Apollo Trampler’s slightly wider build, high-speed lane changes feel easier and more fluid, making the bike feel slightly more flickable on open roads. In city conditions, the tyres feel light and easy to manage, allowing the bike to weave through traffic without requiring extra effort at the bars.

However, there are a couple of trade-offs. Under hard braking, the SCRs feel a bit vague and don’t inspire the same level of confidence, especially when braking aggressively. Highway runs also reveal higher tyre noise, which is likely due to the block-style tread pattern. At urban speeds, though, this noise isn’t very noticeable.

Fuel efficiency has taken a mild hit as well. Where the bike earlier returned around 22-23kmpl, it now consistently delivers close to 20kmpl, translating to a drop of roughly 1-2kmpl.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip Trailhound SCR Long-Term Review: 3 Months & 3,000km Done  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
After nearly 3,000km of city commuting and highway touring, the Eurogrip Trailhound SCRs come across as decent all-rounders for the price they command. They’re easily available through dealerships and the brand’s official website, and they offer stable, predictable road manners with a few compromises in braking feel, noise, and efficiency.

Going forward, apart from continued city and highway use, my aim over the next few months will be to take the bike more off-road and onto light trails to see how these tyres perform beyond the tarmac. That phase of testing should reveal whether the Trailhound SCRs can truly live up to their dual-purpose promise.

page_chunks.title: Reise x Spidi Diablo Pants Long-Term Review  - ZigWheels (part 1)
page_chunks.content:
BluArmor C30 review - Desi helmet communicator for the win?

- Apr 24, 2023
- Views : 6096

I've been using the Reise x Spidi Diablo pants for the past 8 months. During this time, I've used these pants for long rides, off-road trails, some local competition and have had small spills. Here's what my experience with them has been like:

The stitching hasn't come out in any places, and the pants do look and feel almost as good as new. The velcro strap at the waist also sticks rather well and stays in place firmly.

The Diablo pants have been designed with comfort and ventilation in mind. The mesh panels on the thighs and shin provide good levels of ventilation, making riding for long hours in the summer heat quite a pleasant experience. While not designed for off-roading, the pants do fairly well in harsher riding scenarios as well. The lightweight construction, combined with the good ventilation, prevents overheating and fatigue.

page_chunks.title: Reise x Spidi Diablo Pants Long-Term Review  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
The pants have only one pocket on the right, which can be used to store your phone. For my weekend rides, I often carry a waist bag for carrying my phone and wallet. The lack of pockets is one reason why I don't prefer to use them daily. Lastly, the Diablo pants also don't have a connecting zip to attach your riding jacket.

Over the past couple of months, I have begun riding more off-road. If there's one thing that makes off-road riding unique, it's the higher frequency of crashes and falls, albeit usually at slow speeds.

Naturally, I was bound for a spill or two, and in both cases, the Diablo pants saved me from getting severely injured.

While practising at a local dirt track, I had a low-side crash. The CE level 2 protectors at the knee absorbed the impact well, and I was able to walk away unharmed.

page_chunks.title: Reise x Spidi Diablo Pants Long-Term Review  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
The second crash happened during a local race. I have been struggling with right-hand turns since I started riding off-road, and this race was no exception. Poor throttle control and improper vision led me to fall towards the end of the event. This time, my knee hit solid concrete, and once again the pants did their job, allowing me to get back on my feet quickly and start the bike. And despite the two encounters, you would be hard pressed to find any signs of extreme wear and tear on the trousers, just going to show how well the construction actually is.

At a price of Rs 7,999, the Diablo pants are in the accessible riding pants range. From what I've experienced so far, it manages to tick quite a few boxes. Build quality, comfort, ventilation, and, even though I didn’t plan on testing this aspect, protection are all encompassed rather well.

page_chunks.title: Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 First Look: Detailed Walkaround - EICMA 2026 (part 2)
page_chunks.content: Harley-Davidson has unveiled an all-new entry-level cruiser bike called the Sprint 440 at EICMA 2026. Developed in partnership with Hero MotoCorp, the new motorcycle aims to make the Harley-Davidson experience more accessible to a wider audience. Unlike the larger and more imposing motorcycles that the brand is known for, the Sprint 440 gets a lightweight, narrow profile and a relatively low seat height, making it more approachable for everyday riding. Powering the Sprint 440 is a 440cc, single-cylinder engine that produces 27 PS and 38 Nm. It is the same unit which also powers the X440 and is a long-stroke motor has been tuned to deliver strong low-end torque, making it suitable for city riding and relaxed highway cruising. It gets a six-speed gearbox and an assist-and-slipper clutch. The motorcycle also gets 43mm inverted fork, twin shock absorbers with preload adjustment and disc brakes at both ends with ABS.

page_chunks.title: Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 First Look: Detailed Walkaround - EICMA 2026 (part 3)
page_chunks.content: Other highlights include lightweight 10-spoke alloy wheels, a 320mm front disc brake and a relatively accessible riding position. Harley-Davidson has also focused on giving the Sprint 440 a distinctive exhaust note to retain some of the brand's signature character. The Sprint 440 makes its public debut at EICMA 2026, with global dealership availability planned across different markets. Its India launch timeline and pricing have not yet been announced. page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Tell Me About The XEV 9e’s Looks!**

- The XEV 9e is based on the XUV e9 concept car in its design but is based on the brand new all-electric INGLO platform
- It measures just under 4.8 metres in length and is a great example of having large dimensions helps deliver the best results for the coupe-SUV body style
- Ground clearance (unladen) stands at 207mm while its battery pack sits higher with 222mm of clearance
- Owing to its large size (94mm longer than even the XUV700), it looks best with the optional 20-inch alloy wheels but is also offered with 19-inch wheels
- The front end sports vertically-stacked full LED headlights and LED DRLs that run across the entirety of the SUV’s face
- Towards the side, you will notice the flush-fitting front door handles and hidden rear door handles.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

The design is clean and from the side, you get the full effect of the XEV 9e’s size!
- Much like the front, the rear end has a very distinctive connected LED light signature making it impossible to mistake the XEV 9e as anything else
- The 19-inch wheels while styled well look a little small under this near 5 metre long car

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Interiors

**What’s The XEV 9e Like Inside?**

- The base dashboard seems to be a lift off the XUV700 but everything else in the cabin of the XEV 9e is brand new
- A major visual highlight is the triple screen setup that measures around 43 inches across
- The AC control console from the XUV700 also makes way for a piano black touch-panel with shortcuts for a few functions
- The cabin plastics feel smooth and leatherette padding has been used generously to deliver a premium experience
- Steering mounted controls often make you click the horn accidentally
- Piano black control panel under the central AC vents can be very fidgety to use as the icons for the hazard lights or 360-degree camera don’t always click on the first try
- You have to mind your head while getting in as the roofline swoops down sharply

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## Space & Practicality

**Is It Spacious?**

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Space & Practicality

- The XEV 9e puts its size to good use offering great cabin space even for tall users
- Even with the sloping roof line, there is good headroom for users up to or a little over 6ft in height
- Thanks to the flat floor, seating 3 occupants at the rear is also comfortable so long as the users are of an average build
- Rear seat users can adjust the backrest angle and the front passenger’s seat can be adjusted from the rear seat using a lever too
- The door pockets are large enough to accommodate big bottles and there’s a large space between the front passengers to store more items
- Without the parcel cover in place, there’s enough room to fit 2 large suitcases into the boot
- The boot space is rated at 663 litres but with the sloping roofline, there’s only space for one full-sized suitcase with the roller-type parcel cover in use
- The XUV700, a car that’s a little smaller in size than the XEV 9e can seat 7 while this is a 5 seater only with a boot that’s isn’t bigger either

- Powered front seat with driver memory
- Ventilated front seats
- Powered tailgate
- Wireless phone charger
- Front and rear type-C USB chargers (65W)
- Fixed panoramic glass roof
- Auto AC with rear AC vents
- Multi-colour ambient lighting with animation programs
- NFC key card access
- Tilt & telescopic steering adjustment
- Drive modes

- No full sized spare tyre, just a 135/80 R18 space saver spare tyre

page_chunks.content:
## Infotainment

**What Infotainment Features Does The XEV 9e Offer?**

- 12.3 inch digital instrument cluster with multi-views and real-time ADAS display
- 12.3 inch touchscreen infotainment system with wireless Android Auto/Apple CarPlay
- 16-speaker Harman Kardon music system that delivers excellent sound quality
- On-board selfie camera with photo and video modes
- The front passenger’s screen can be used to view content on YouTube or OTT apps, play games and it even links to the interior camera for video calls on Zoom or Google Meets
- Groove Me light and music show that engages the exterior lights, ambient lights, pop-out door handles and wing mirrors
- Digital instrument cluster response times could’ve been quicker
- The front passenger’s screen remains active even when the car is on the move which can be distracting for the driver

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Battery & Charging

**Talk About Charging The XEV 9e**

- Using a 175kW charger, the 79kWh battery can go from 20-80 percent charge in 20 minutes
- Using a 140kW charger, the 59kWh battery can go from 20-80 percent charge in 20 minutes
- With the optional 11kW AC fast charger, the XEV 9e can be charged from 0-100 percent in 6-8 hours (59-79kWh batteries respectively)
- With the optional 7kW AC fast charger, the XEV 9e can be charged from 0-100 percent in 9-12 hours (59-79kWh batteries respectively)
- Claimed range for the 79kWh battery pack stands at 682km though it should manage 500-550km in real-world conditions
- Claimed range for the 59kWh battery pack stands at 535km though it should manage 380-450km in real-world conditions
- While charging options for the car are vast, the public charging infrastructure is still often inconsistent and not dependable in many locations

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 16)
page_chunks.content:
## Safety

**What About Safety Features?**

- Features include ABS with EBD, ESP. 7 airbags, front and rear parking sensors, ISOFIX child seat mounts, all-wheel disc brakes
- Also gets 360-degree camera with indicator linked display in the instrument cluster
- 360-degree camera includes Secure360 which keeps monitoring on even when the car is switched off
- Advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) include auto-braking, adaptive cruise control, lane-assist, auto lane-switch and overtaking, rear crossing traffic alert and high-beam assist
- Auto park assist which can be operated from the key, phone app or while seated in the car.
- Supports parallel, perpendicular or angular parking possible
- Auto-park assist doesn’t account for changes in road depth and may not work correctly where road-level changes are involved

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 17)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Range

**Will I Like Driving The XEV 9e?**

- The XEV 9e is offered with two battery packs - 59kWh or 79kWh
- Offered only with rear-wheel drive, the motor makes 230PS with the smaller battery and 285PS with the bigger battery. Both versions offer 380Nm of torque
- The XEV 9e is both quick and smooth to drive, with gentle power delivery for city commutes and punch for high speed overtaking
- 0-100kmph takes a claimed 6.8 seconds only!
- One-pedal driving and regen calibration is smooth. First time electric car buyers can get used to the experience quickly

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 18)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**About The Handling And Comfort**

- Steering is light to use and makes controlling this large car easy
- Handling is predictable too and it feels sharp at high speeds or while cornering
- Noise insulation is great and keeps you relaxed during long commutes
- Ride comfort is something the XEV 9e delivers in spades and even sharp potholes don’t unsettle the cabin
- While being soft enough to handle bad roads, it’s also not too soft or bouncy while driving at highway speeds

page_chunks.title: Mahindra XEV 9e 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 19)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Who Should Buy The Mahindra XEV 9e?**

- The XEV 9e is an electric SUV that makes for a sensible style statement.
- While it looks like a lifestyle SUV, at its core it’s a comfortable, spacious and practical car for the family
- The cherry on top is the tech package that’s more elaborate and loaded than what some luxury SUVs offer while charging more than double the price
- Additionally, the performance is as exciting as it is usable with battery pack options that’ll manage a real-world range of 400-550km quite easily
- The Mahindra XEV 9e is an SUV truly built to global standards. What remains to be seen is if the full range of variants is still offered at a reasonably India-friendly price

## Design

**Distinct But Eye-catching Design**

- Aerodynamic, egg-like shape with modern-looking connected LED DRLs and sleek LED headlights.
- Illuminated MG logo on the bonnet looks beautiful at night.
- Flush-fitting door handles and huge 18-inch alloy wheels gives it an upmarket feel.
- Does not get a rear wiper or washer even in its top variant.
- Unique road presence but fails to be as commanding as an SUV.

page_chunks.title: MG Windsor EV 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## Interiors

**Minimalist But A Premium Cabin**

- Premium cabin with soft-touch materials on the doors and dashboard.
- An extensive usage of faux wood trims and rose gold accents exude a premium appeal.
- Minimalist layout with a 2-spoke steering wheel, a massive touchscreen, a touch-enabled AC control panel and a digital driver’s display.
- Some lightweight plastics used in the centre console and door handles reduce the upmarket feel.
- Touchscreen controls and minimal physical buttons can feel complicated to use. Can be tricky to explain if other members in the family use the same car.

page_chunks.title: MG Windsor EV 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Space & Practicality

**Very Practical For A Family Of 5**

- Spacious interior with seating for 5 and comfortable rear seats that recline up to 135 degrees.
- Up to 604-litre boot space with adjustable floor, easily accommodates an entire suitcase set along with some smaller soft bags.
- Cabin has great storage options including multiple cup holders for all passengers and a large center console storage compartment.
- Charging sockets in the front console storage compartment are not easily accessible.
- Rear AC vent only directs airflow to one side.

page_chunks.title: MG Windsor EV 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:

**Feature Loaded To Its Gills**

- Massive 15.6-inch touchscreen that is bright and presents good colours and supports wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay.
- Smaller 8.8-inch digital driver’s display with multiple display layouts but no support for navigation on it.
- Excellent 9-speaker Infinity sound system that gives a bass-heavy audio experience.
- Other highlights: Panoramic glass roof, 64-colour ambient lighting, 6-way power adjustable driver’s seat and ventilated front seats.
- The 'Pro Variant also gets powered tailgate as well as Level-2 ADAS
- Most of the controls are on the touchscreen which take some time getting used to.

**What About Safety Features?**

- 6 airbags, rear parking sensors, tyre pressure monitoring system (TPMS) and an electronic parking brake provided as standard.
- Higher variants add a 360-degree camera and rear defogger to the mix.
- 'Pro' variant offers Level-2 ADAS Tech

page_chunks.title: MG Windsor EV 2026 Price, Range, Charging Time & Specs | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Range

**A Decent Performer**

- Gets a 38 kWh battery mated to a FWD motor that produces 136 PS and 200 Nm.
- Claimed range of 331km with real-world expected range closer to 260-280 km.
- Four driving modes: Eco Plus, Eco, Normal, and Sport.
- Sport mode offers quicker acceleration, but is not thrilling in any manner.
- The 'Pro' variant with the bigger battery pack, offers a real-world range of about 350-360 km, which is about 100 km more than the regualr Windsor EV
- Regenerative braking adjustable through touchscreen which can be cumbersome due to the lack of any physical control.
- Efficient and predictable throttle response for city and highway driving, but lacks excitement.

- Gets a larger 52.9 kWh battery (up from 40.55 kWh in the standard Windsor).

**Good Things**

- Unique looks, great build quality
- Impressive list of features and plush spacious interiors
- Unique warranty, buy-back and free charging options for new customers

- Rear seat recline is comfortable but does eat into boot space

With a real-world range of around 250-260km, it is a great city runabout. Now, with the Pro variant in picture, it does offer a decent real-world range of 350-360 km, but unfortunately, it is only limited to the top-end variant.
