page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Tell Me About The Toyota Camry’s Looks!**

- All-new design gives the Camry a sporty edge that it didn’t have before
- New ‘hammer head’ face looks much sharper and aero inspired than before
- DRL signature is quite unique and looks great on the road
- 18-inch dual tone alloy wheels look sporty yet traditional.
- The all-black alloy wheels from the Sprint Edition pack look even nicer and should be available on the accessories catalog
- Sprint Edition adds front and rear bumper extensions, ORVM and roof matt black wrap and all-black alloy and looks more sporty, especially in this red
- It is available in 6 colours that include a cement grey, black, dark blue, red, white and steel grey.
- Sprint Edition bumper wasn’t perfectly fit which isn’t surprising considering it is a dealer fitted pack
- Might not look as young and sporty as the small German luxury sedans

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## Interiors

**What’s The Camry Like Inside?**

- Black and tan interior theme is plush and upmarket in both feeling and fit and finish
- Finally Toyota has delivered a contemporary looking dash design which is simple and attractive
- Physical buttons means that it’s easy to operate the air con and the ventilated front seats
- At the rear there is plenty of space on offer too with electronically reclining seats, electric rear sun screen and manual side sunshades. All neatly controlled by a touch panel on the centre armrest.
- Rear passengers can also control the media via the touch remote.
- Dual rear entertainment screens are also part of the accessory catalog
- Piano black elements will be finger print and dust magnets

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Space & Practicality

**Is the Camry Spacious?**

- Space has always been one of the Camry’s highlights and that theme continues with the new generation.
- Plenty of leg, foot and head room in the rear seats despite the low profile and sloping sedan roof.
- Storage and connectivity options are available in good measure all around the cabin.

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## Space & Practicality

Point to note that all the charge points are type-C.
- Boot is a generous 587-litres on paper and should hold whatever you need to carry
- Should be able to easily fit a golf set in here two because the armrest does open up to allow this, or access to items in the boot from the inside of the car.
- 10-way electric driver seat adjustment and electronic tilt and telescopic steering allows anyone to find their perfect driving position.
- Seats are also super comfortable and supportive with ventilation in the front row
- It’s a sedan so you do need to step down into the car and getting out will be a little more tiresome for the elderly
- Rear armrest on all the drive cars didn't seem to fit flush when folded away. Not really an issue but something that a keen eye will easily pick out, and then won’t be able to unsee.

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

**What Features Does The Camry Offer?**

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

- Dual 12.3 inch screens for the infotainment and drivers dash are snappy and clear.
- The head-up display is crisp, simple and works well.
- Drivers dash has one of the most customisable interfaces we have come across. You can arrange info to be displayed in multiple locations and you can even save your favourite layouts
- 9-speaker JBL audio system has good clarity and even sounds great at higher volumes.
- 360-degree camera quality is great
- Other worthy mentions include 3-zones of climate control, auto IRVM, sunroof, wireless phone charging and wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay, auto wipers and auto headlamps.
- The infotainment interface lacks a home button and defaults to the map view which feels odd. Interface is shallow in depth with few options to play around with
- 360 degree camera only comes on when reverse is engaged. It can be activated by a button on the right hand console but then only has limited functionality and less customisation.

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Safety

**The Camry’s Safety Features**

- Great safety package that includes 9-airbags, ISOFIX mounts and level-2 ADAS
- Received a 5 star rating from ANCAP

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**Will I Like Driving The Camry?**

- Powering the Camry is the same 2.5-litre four-cylinder petrol motor paired with an electric motor. The combined power output is 230PS and 221Nm.
- It makes 12PS more than the previous generation powertrain and Toyota is claiming 25.29 kmpl in terms of efficiency.
- Self charging hybrid technology means you only need to worry about filling up fuel. No need to worry about charging up the batteries
- Acceleration is brisk and the claimed figure of 7.2 seconds to 100kmph is believable
- Drive experience is smooth and the camry feels quick when you are cruising on the highway and making overtakes.
- Engine noise and vibration is well insulated
- CVT gearbox isn’t happy with full throttle inputs and will then punish your enthusiasm with a stark rise in RPM, but slow rise in actual speed
- 10-step CVT only gives you ten steps at part throttle. Push harder on the gas and the gear paddles are practically meaningless.

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 16)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

The transmission will spin up and drone on until you back off the throttle and this happens even in manual override mode.
- A little more road noise was noticeable at cruise speeds on the highway than we’d expect from such a plush car.

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 17)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort & Storage

**Is It A Comfortable Car?**

- The ride and driving experience makes cruising down an open highway a very enjoyable experience
- Still one of the best riding cars for the money despite the rather low profile 235/45 R18 wheels
- With the new generation the handling has improved so it’s a more enjoyable experience when the roads turn a little twisty too
- Ground clearance seems adequate for normal roads and speed bumps.
- Not the enthusiasts choice for driving experience
- Will still have to be careful over bad roads and large speed bumps

page_chunks.title: Toyota Camry 2026 Price, Variants, Mileage, Specs & Colours | ZigWheels (part 18)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Why Should I Buy The Toyota Camry?**

- It is a considerable step-up in every department compared to the outgoing car
- Packs in more features, is a better driving experience and is quicker and more efficient too.
- Looks and design both inside and out have really taken the ‘Camry’ experience forward
- For the money it’s asking for and the overall experience its offering, the Toyota Camry could seriously tempt buyers away from some luxury brands.
- If you must spend over Rs 50 lakhs on a premium experience that borders on luxury, and gives you the peace of mind that the Toyota badge does, the Camry ticks a heck of a lot of boxes.

- Positives
- Negatives

- Updated styling isn’t as polarizing - Looks expensive!

- Loaded with features like dual 10.25” displays & Level 2 ADAS & panoramic sunroof etc

- Looks aggressive and has strong road presence.
- Cabin space is accommodating for a family of 5.
- 6 airbags, ABS with EBD, ISOFIX, rear camera, TPMS and a lot more safety as standard. Higher variants add ADAS, 360-degree camera and more!

- Feature-rich: 30-inch panoramic display, 8-speaker BOSE music system, ventilated front seats, powered driver’s seat with memory, panoramic sunroof and a lot more.

- Limited variants for automatic - Turbo engine available in a single automatic variant

Last Updated: November 16, 2026

If you're deciding between the Slavia and Virtus, the Slavia is the better pick for affordability, while the Virtus stands out for performance.

## Overview

**Still the King?**

- The Hero Splendor Plus XTEC stands out as a more premium version of the iconic Splendor Plus
- The bike features a digital instrument console and a few other changes compared to the standard Splendor
- But does the bike offer enough to stand apart and still appeal to the average consumer? We will be answering this question.

page_chunks.title: Hero Splendor Plus XTEC Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**A More Premium Splendor Plus?**

- The Hero Splendor Plus XTEC has not received a radical change in design when compared to the standard Hero Splendor Plus.
- The bike still maintains that iconic square headlight, boxy-looking tank and an overall slim profile
- The XTEC variant gets slightly more premium looking colours and styling, which manages to make the bike feel a bit more premium

page_chunks.title: Hero Splendor Plus XTEC Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**The cheapest bike to run?**

- Powered by a 97.2cc, air-cooled, single-cylinder engine which produces 8.02PS and 8.05Nm. The power and torque are adequate to keep up with city traffic
- Has enough bottom-end grunt to execute quick overtakes in city traffic
- Offers an incredible tested mileage of 83.2kmpl in the city and 95.8kmpl on the highway
- Refinement is not the best and vibrations can be felt when pushing the bike upwards of 80kmph

page_chunks.title: Hero Splendor Plus XTEC Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**The best city bike?**

- Feels very light and agile when riding in city traffic conditions, and the small size makes it easy to cut through traffic
- The light weight of 112kg makes it easy to move around in the parking lot
- The drum brakes do not inspire confidence when riding in the city. For better braking performance, riders will have to get the XTEC disc variant
- The rear brakes do not offer much feel, so it is easy to lock up the rear during emergency braking situations

page_chunks.title: Hero Splendor Plus XTEC Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:

**A comfortable ride?**

- The Splendor XTEC’s suspension setup is set towards the stiffer side and the ride quality is not the best. You will feel a lot of the bumps and potholes on the road
- The suspension setup only balances out when riding with a pillion or heavier loads

page_chunks.title: Hero Splendor Plus XTEC Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:

**Relaxed but not the most comfortable**

- The bike offers a relatively upright riding posture which is quite relaxed and comfortable
- The low seat height also makes it easy for shorter riders to get their feet down
- The seat cushioning is on the softer side which makes short rides in the city very comfortable
- The soft seat doesn't do a good job supporting the rider’s weight for longer distances. After a while, the rider’s butt starts sinking into the foam making the ride uncomfortable

- USB charging port is a very convenient addition which makes charging on the go easy

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## Overview

**Everyones favourite Royal Enfield**

- The Classic 350 is Royal Enfield’s most popular and highest selling motorcycle
- It has retained its classic design right from when it was originally launched in 2009
- The Classic 350 is known for its easy-going nature
- It's the preferred bike for many for riding to Ladakh, thanks to its torquey engine and ease of carrying heavy loads

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Timelessly Classic**

- Timeless, retro looks make it look beautiful from all angles
- The round LED headlight with the tiger lamps accentuate the retro aspect of the roadster very well
- It gets stylish colour options with premium badging that make the bike look premium
- And yes, the Classic 350 is available in green. Royal Enfield calls it the Gorkha Edition, designed as a tribute to the Gorkha regiment.
- The classic design won’t appeal to those who like modern-looking motorcycles

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**Torquey & Tractable**

- Powered by a 349cc, air-oil cooled engine producing 20.21PS at 6100rpm and 27Nm at 4000rpm
- Comes with a 5-speed gearbox along with a slip and assist clutch
- Motor offers smooth performance and can sustain speeds of 100kmph comfortably
- Motor is very tractable, making the retro roadster easy to ride in the city
- Returned mileage of 41.55kmpl in city and 37.77kmpl on highway in our tests, which is quite good for a 350cc bike
- Post 100kmph, some vibrations start to creep in; 80-90kmph is the sweet spot for the bike
- Doesn’t have the iconic 'thump' of the older Classic but still has a sweet sounding exhaust note

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**Easygoing manners**

- The Classic 350 has neutral handling characteristics and is quite easy to manoeuvre in city traffic conditions
- Requires a bit of effort to tip the bike into corners but it is not a deal breaker
- The initial bite from the brakes could have been better

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Ride Quality

**Handles all roads**

- The telescopic fork and twin shock absorbers suspension setup handles bumps and potholes quite well
- With a ground clearance of 170mm, the Classic 350 tackles speed breakers easily
- The rear suspension setup is a bit on the firmer side, meaning undulations can be felt while riding over bad roads at high speeds

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 16)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort & Storage

**Built for comfort**

- Gets a relaxed and upright riding posture with an easy to reach handlebar and mid-set footpegs
- Comfortable for commuting on a daily basis as well as for touring and the occasional highway rides
- Despite the 805mm seat height, riders of all heights and can easily plant both feet flat on the ground
- Stock seat is a bit too soft, better to upgrade to the touring seat
- Still feels quite heavy when parking or moving with your feet

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 17)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

**Like a mechanical watch**

- The roadster gets a semi-digital instrument console with an analogue speedometer looks properly retro
- Digital inset that shows odometer, trip meter and fuel gauge readouts is good to have
- All-LED lighting and a USB Type-C fast charging port is available as standard for the dual-channel ABS variants
- Tripper navigation pod for turn-by-turn navigation is now standard on the Emerald and Stealth colour options
- The Classic 350 is still not as feature rich as some of the bikes in the same price range

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 18)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Is the Royal Enfield Classic 350 worth it?**

- The Royal Enfield Classic 350 has dominated the sub-400cc retro roadster segment in the Indian two-wheeler market for years now and rightfully so. It offers the perfect blend of gorgeous retro looks, smooth and relaxed performance, comfortable riding experience and features list that is adequate for a retro roadster. If you are a fan of retro motorcycles, then the Classic 350 is one of the best options to consider for your next purchase.

page_chunks.content:
## Overview

**The Most Affordable RE**

- The Royal Enfield Hunter 350 is a 350cc neo-retro roadster bike
- It is the most affordable bike from the Royal Enfield
- It is also the most lightweight Royal Enfield bike till date

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Hunter 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**More Neo - Less Retro**

- The Hunter 350 comes with a neo-retro roadster design that looks good
- The bike comes with a teardrop-shaped sculpted fuel tank that complements the overall design
- The Hunter 350 has round headlight, mirrors, indicators and even the instrument console
- It comes in 10 vibrant colour schemes
- The modern(ish) design and youthful colours might not appeal to hardcore Royal Enfield fans
- The Hunter 350 is very compact as compared to other Royal Enfield bikes

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Hunter 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**An Impressive City Commuter**

- The Hunter gets the same 350cc single-cylinder J-series engine as the Classic 350, Bullet 350 and Meteor 350
- However, the engine feels different on the Hunter as it has been tuned accordingly
- Thanks to the torquey engine, it rides comfortably at lower speeds in higher gears
- In our tests, it delivered a mileage of 40.19kmpl in the city and 35.98kmpl out on the highway
- The top-end performance of the Hunter 350 is not that impressive
- The bike feels stressed after 90kmph and reaching triple-digit speeds is a task

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Hunter 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**Lightest Royal Enfield In The Market**

- The Hunter 350 handles very well and is a fun-to-ride bike
- Because of its lightweight and 17-inch wheels, it feels very light to ride around compared to other REs
- It doesn’t have the agility of a sporty streetfighter but for a retro roadster, it's quite impressive
- The tyres are just about ok. Better tyres would make the handling even more confidence-inspiring

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Hunter 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Ride Quality

**Turns Bad on Bad Roads**

- The Royal Enfield Hunter 350 has a hint of commitment in its riding posture, making it engaging to ride
- It takes on the corners and twisties very well, thanks to the sharp handling
- The rear suspension is set up rather stiff and feels jarring on bad roads
- The brakes have a decent bite, but the levers feel spongy while braking

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Hunter 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 16)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort & Storage

**Not something to boast about**

- Hunter 350’s riding posture is similar to modern-day street bikes with a slight forward lean, but is comfortable
- The rider section of the seat is quite spacious

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Hunter 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 17)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

**Has Only What’s Necessary**

- The Hunter 350 gets an off-set semi-digital instrument console, borrowed from the Scram 411
- The LCD console has small text which is hard to read while riding
- The Hunter 350 misses out on ride modes, and smartphone connectivity features
- The tripper navigation pod is only available as an optional feature

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Hunter 350 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 18)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Should You Buy the Royal Enfield Hunter 350?**

- The Royal Enfield Hunter 350 can be a friendly beginner bike for someone who likes neo-retro roadsters
- It can be a good bike for everyday use, but you will have to deal with the firm ride quality
- It may not be very impressive in terms of performance and features, but the affordable price tag makes it desirable
- The Hunter 350’s prices undercut all its rivals and are on par with the 226cc TVS Ronin

page_chunks.title: Yamaha R15 V4 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Peak of sportiness**

- The R15 V4 has a very aggressive supersport design and styling, which takes inspiration from Yamaha’s higher capacity bikes like the R7
- The gold-finished inverted fork on select colours also adds a bit more premiumness to the bike overall
- The sharp looking rear section gives the bike a very sporty character
- The halogen turn-indicators that stick out of the fairing takes away from the bike’s premium look and feel

page_chunks.title: Yamaha R15 V4 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**Peak of rev happiness**

- The Yamaha R15’s 155cc, liquid-cooled, single-cylinder engine outputs 18.4PS and 14.2Nm, and offers linear acceleration and power delivery
- The engine is quite rev happy and most of the power and torque is produced at the higher rpm. This makes it really nice to ride on the twisties and also on the track
- The quickshifter is quite smooth and easy to use. In the standard variant, it is available in Matte Pearl White, Racing Blue, and Intensity White colours.
- Offers a tested mileage of 55.20kmpl on the city
- Doesn’t have much power and torque at the lower rev ranges, and the engine only feels alive once it revs above 7,000rpm

page_chunks.title: Yamaha R15 V4 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**The perfect cornering weapon?**

- The bike feels quite at place in the twisties and tips into corners effortlessly
- The suspension is set towards the stiffer side and this helps in improving the bike’s sporty handling characteristic
- Feels quite agile and the smaller profile makes it easier to manoeuvre through city traffic
- Braking hardware could have been better and offered a bit stronger initial bite

page_chunks.title: Yamaha R15 V4 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:

**Too sporty for its own good?**

- The stiffer suspension does manage to soak up most bumps and potholes on the road and is reasonable for a supersport

page_chunks.title: Yamaha R15 V4 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:

**Not the most relaxed**

- The clip-ons are slightly raised so riders won’t have to lean in too much to get the optimal riding posture
- The tank panels also make it easier to hold the bike with one’s knees during cornering
- The riding posture is still quite sporty and many riders will struggle with it

page_chunks.title: Yamaha R15 V4 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:

**Has enough of them**

- The negatively-lit LCD instrument console offers smartphone connectivity and related features such call/SMS alerts and turn-by-turn navigation

page_chunks.title: Yamaha R15 V4 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Worth the buy?**

- The Yamaha R15 stands out as a really good entry level supersport, which manages to offer good looks and performance. The refined nature of the engine, and linear power delivery makes the bike a good choice for beginners. The bike also has a few practical features which will make it quite good in the city. Overall, the bike will be perfect for those riders who are looking for their first supersport on which they can improve their riding skills. More experienced riders on the other hand will be better off with a higher capacity bike which can offer greater performance.

- The design language, inspired by Yamaha's larger sport bikes, will surely appeal to enthusiasts

- Despite its sporty performance, the R15 offers decent mileage, making it usable for daily commuting
- The top-spec M variant is the only bike in the segment to get a quickshifter

- The aggressive riding position may not be suitable for all riders, especially for long-duration rides

## Pulsar N160 S Key Highlights

**Features:**
The Pulsar N160 S gets an electronic ride-by-wire throttle, which enables multiple riding aids: Rain, Sport, Road and Off-road. There’s also a low-rpm assist.
Both its variants get a digital display; the N160 S variant has an LCD console with Bluetooth connectivity enabling turn-by-turn navigation and phone alerts. The N160 SS variant gets a 5-inch TFT console with Bluetooth plus Wi-Fi connectivity, and it can also mirror Google Maps navigation (first in segment).
The top SS variant also gets better safety features with dual-channel ABS and traction control, which the base N160 S misses out on.

**Engine:**
This Pulsar N160 gets a new 165cc air-oil-cooled, 4-valve engine. This engine makes 18.5 PS at 9,500 rpm and 14.4 Nm at 8,000 rpm, paired with a 5-speed gearbox. Bajaj claims that it accelerates from 0 to 40 kmph in 4.5 seconds.

The bike is equipped with a 37mm USD fork and monoshock. It has a 14-litre fuel tank and 165mm ground clearance – same as the standard Pulsar N160. The seat height is 795 mm and the kerb weight stands at 151 kg.
The bike rolls on 17-inch tyres at both ends with 110/80-section front and 130/70 rear radial tyres. Braking is managed by 300mm front and 230mm rear disc brakes.

**Rivals:**
The Pulsar N160 S and SS rival the TVS Apache RTR 160 4V, and Hero Xtreme 160R 4V.

**Variants:**
The Bajaj Pulsar N160 S is available in two variants, the base S variant and the top SS variant.

## Overview

**Tiger 1200 Overview**

- The new Triumph Tiger 1200 gets significant updates to its engine, chassis, suspension and technology package.
- Its 1160cc, three-cylinder engine now produces 158PS and 130Nm, with improved low-speed performance and refinement.
- The updated suspension, automatic seat-lowering function and radar-based rider assistance systems make it more accessible and technologically advanced.
- The Tiger 1200 is offered in two variants in India: GT Pro (Rs 20,99,000 ex-showroom Delhi), and Rally Explorer (Rs 23,49,000 ex-showroom Delhi), with different wheel types, fuel tank capacities and off-road equipment.

## Design

**Tiger 1200 Design**

- The new Tiger 1200 retains its distinctive adventure motorcycle silhouette but gets redesigned bodywork for a sharper and more modern appearance.
- The revised fuel tank, radiator cowls, front beak and windscreen give the motorcycle a more muscular look.
- It gets an LED projector headlight with adaptive cornering functionality, along with a new DRL and separate LED marker lights.
- The rear features multifunction LED units that integrate the indicators and tail-lights for a cleaner finish.
- The GT Pro gets cast aluminium wheels for a sportier, road-focused appearance, while the Rally Explorer features side-laced spoked wheels for a more rugged, off-road-ready look.

## Performance & Mileage

**Tiger 1200 Performance & Mileage**

- The Tiger 1200 is powered by a 1160cc, liquid-cooled, three-cylinder engine that produces 158PS at 9,250rpm and 130Nm at 6,750rpm.
- The updated engine produces 8PS more than before, while revisions to the cylinder head, pistons, valves, fuel injection and exhaust are aimed at improving combustion efficiency and performance.
- The engine delivers more torque at lower revs, making slow-speed riding and tight manoeuvres easier to manage.
- The six-speed gearbox and shaft drive have been refined for smoother operation, more precise gear selection and cleaner transitions between acceleration and deceleration.
- The motorcycle also gets a bidirectional quickshifter, allowing faster clutchless gear changes in both directions.
- The low-maintenance shaft drive reduces the need for regular chain cleaning and adjustment, making it useful for long-distance touring.

## Handling

**Tiger 1200 Handling**

- The Tiger 1200 gets a revised chassis setup with a 19-inch front wheel and a 17-inch rear wheel across both models.
- The 200mm suspension travel at both ends, lightweight chassis construction and Tri-Link aluminium swingarm are designed to improve agility and provide precise handling feedback.
- The GT Pro's cast aluminium wheels give it a more road-biased setup, while the Rally Explorer's spoked wheels and additional off-road equipment cater to riders who want more off-road capability.
- The Brembo Stylema brakes, twin 320mm front discs and Optimised Cornering ABS provide braking support, with the system using wheel-speed data and information from a six-axis IMU.
- The semi-active suspension continuously adjusts compression and rebound damping using real-time sensor inputs, helping the motorcycle remain composed over uneven surfaces and under braking.

- The Tiger 1200 uses Showa Eera Heightflex semi-active suspension, which offers three damping settings: Firm, Medium and Soft.

- A hydraulic secondary bump stop provides additional control on more demanding terrain.
- Both models get 200mm of suspension travel at the front and rear, while the suspension setup is designed to balance road handling with off-road capability.
- The revised engine, gearbox and shaft drive are also aimed at reducing mechanical harshness and making the overall riding experience smoother.

## Overview

**Duke 200 Overview**

- The KTM 200 Duke received a significant update in October 2026, with new electronic rider aids, two new colours and hardware improvements.
- The updated motorcycle gets ride-by-wire, a bidirectional quickshifter, traction control and two riding modes.
- Other additions include 43mm WP upside-down front forks, a larger 320mm front disc brake and a wider 150-section rear tyre.
- The updated KTM 200 Duke is priced at Rs 2,07,140 (ex-showroom Delhi), an increase of Rs 1,552 over the previous version.

page_chunks.title: KTM 200 Duke Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 22)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Duke 200 Design**

- The KTM 200 Duke retains its aggressive streetfighter design, with a sharp fuel tank, muscular tank extensions, exposed frame elements and a compact rear section.
- The latest update introduces two new colour options: Liquid Carbon and Slate Grey.
- Liquid Carbon brings an all-black finish to the 200 Duke for the first time, giving it a more understated appearance while retaining its sporty character.
- Slate Grey offers a contrasting look, adding another styling option to the motorcycle's existing colour palette.
- The large fork and wide rear tyre also contribute to a more muscular appearance.

page_chunks.title: KTM 200 Duke Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 23)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**Duke 200 Performance & Mileage**

- The KTM 200 Duke has a 199.5cc, liquid-cooled, single-cylinder engine, producing 25PS at 10,000rpm and 19.3Nm at 8,000rpm, paired with a six-speed gearbox.
- The latest update introduces ride-by-wire technology, which uses electronic throttle control instead of a conventional mechanical throttle.
- The update also added a bidirectional quickshifter, allowing clutchless upshifts and downshifts, making gear changes quicker without requiring the rider to operate the clutch lever for every shift.
- The new Street and Rain riding modes allow riders to adapt the motorcycle's power delivery to different riding conditions, while traction control helps manage rear-wheel grip.

page_chunks.title: KTM 200 Duke Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 24)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**Duke 200 Handling**

- The KTM 200 Duke gets a 43mm WP upside-down fork.
- It also gets a wide 150-section rear tyre.
- The updated motorcycle features a 320mm front brake rotor, offering a larger braking surface than the earlier setup.

page_chunks.title: KTM 200 Duke Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 25)
page_chunks.content:
## Ride Quality

**Duke 200 Ride Quality**

- The new Rain riding mode is designed to adapt power delivery to wet conditions, while traction control helps manage rear-wheel traction.
- The Street mode is intended for regular riding conditions, giving riders an alternative to Rain mode depending on the road and weather.
- Crawl Assist is another new feature highlighted by KTM. It is particularly useful in stop-and-go city traffic, as it is designed to reduce rider fatigue in slow-moving conditions.

page_chunks.title: KTM 200 Duke Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 26)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort & Storage

**Duke 200 Comfort & STorage**

- The KTM 200 Duke retains its sporty streetfighter ergonomics, with an upright handlebar and a riding position intended to balance everyday usability with spirited riding.
- The new Crawl Assist feature is designed to reduce rider fatigue in stop-and-go traffic, making it a useful addition for urban commutes.

page_chunks.title: KTM 200 Duke Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 27)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

**Duke 200 Features**

- The biggest additions are ride-by-wire technology, a bidirectional quickshifter, traction control and two riding modes: Street and Rain. These features are now standard on the updated KTM 200 Duke.
- The updated TFT display allows riders to manage traction control, riding modes and the quickshifter through the instrument interface.
- Crawl Assist is designed to reduce rider fatigue in stop-and-go traffic, adding a practical convenience feature for everyday city riding.
- The motorcycle retains its sporty streetfighter character, while the updated electronic package brings technology previously associated with KTM's larger-capacity motorcycles to the 200 Duke.

page_chunks.title: KTM 200 Duke Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 28)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Duke 200 Verdict**

- The October 2026 update makes the KTM 200 Duke a more feature-rich motorcycle, with ride-by-wire technology, a bi-directional quickshifter, traction control and two riding modes offered as standard.
- Its 199.5cc engine continues to produce 25PS and 19.3Nm, so the focus remains on improving rider control and convenience rather than increasing outright performance.
- The updated hardware package includes 43mm WP upside-down front forks, a 320mm front brake rotor and a wider 150-section rear tyre. Crawl Assist is another useful addition, particularly for riders who regularly deal with stop-and-go city traffic.
- The two new colours, Liquid Carbon and Slate Grey, provide fresh styling options, with Liquid Carbon introducing an all-black finish to the 200 Duke for the first time.
- Priced at Rs 2,07,140 (ex-showroom Delhi), the updated KTM 200 Duke costs just Rs 1,552 more than the previous version.

The small price increase makes the additional electronic features and hardware changes a significant part of its appeal.

**Design:**
Ducati has kept the Hypermotard's double-wing tank and twin under-seat exhausts, but the new bike looks leaner and more compact. The biggest news is weight. The new monocoque frame, which uses the engine as part of the structure, makes the bike up to 14 kg lighter than before. The seat height is 880 mm, which is tall for most riders, so it's worth sitting on one before you book.

page_chunks.content:
## Hypermotard V2 Key Highlights

**Features:**
The electronics have been borrowed from the Panigale V4 playbook and use a 6-axis IMU. The best bit is the "Slide by Brake" function, which lets you slide the rear into corners supermotard-style, while the electronics step in if things go wrong. You also get cornering ABS, traction and wheelie control, an upgraded quickshifter and a new 5-inch TFT with a lap timer. Cruise control and heated grips are optional extras, so this is a bike built for fun and not for touring.

**Engine:**
The new 890cc V-twin makes 120 PS and 94 Nm, and it's the lightest twin-cylinder engine Ducati has ever built. What matters in the real world is that 70 per cent of peak torque is available from just 3,000 rpm, so it should feel strong without having to be revved out. Ducati hasn't shared a mileage figure yet, and the 12.5-litre tank is on the small side.

**Design:**
The Benelli TRK 552 series carries an aggressive, big adventure bike stance, centered around a sharp front beak, a muscular 20-litre fuel tank, and exposed steel tubular trellis frame sections. Up front, it features full-LED lighting with dual headlights, integrated daytime running lights, LED turn signals, and a tall windscreen designed for wind protection. Protection elements include high-mounted crash guards, newly designed handguards, and sturdy rear grab rails. The visual separation between the two models comes down to their wheel configurations: the standard TRK 552 runs 17-inch alloy wheels for a clean road setup, whereas the TRK 552X uses wire-spoke wheels with a larger 19-inch front.

## TRK 552 Key Highlights

**Features:**
The biggest upgrade is the new 5-inch TFT display, which now comes with Bluetooth and navigation. It also supports offline maps, which is a useful bonus on routes where the network drops out. Other highlights include heated grips, a heated seat, a USB charging port, TPMS, a gear indicator, all-LED lighting, and Bosch dual-channel ABS. T-BOX connectivity is on offer as well.

**Engine:**
Both bikes are powered by a 554cc, liquid-cooled parallel-twin engine that makes 53PS and 49 Nm. **Suspension, Brakes & Other Details:**
Both bikes get a 50 mm USD front fork, a preload-adjustable monoshock, twin 320 mm front discs and a 260 mm rear disc, with dual-channel ABS as standard. The wheels are where they differ. The TRK 552 rides on 17-inch alloys with 120/70 front and 160/60 rear Pirelli tyres, a setup better suited to paved roads. ## F 450 R Key Highlights

**Price:**

**Design:**
The BMW F 450 R looks sharp and aggressive, with a stacked twin-pod LED headlight featuring a V-shaped design. The pointy tank extensions, exposed frame and sub-frame give it a proper naked-bike appeal, while the underbelly exhaust elevates its sporty look.

page_chunks.title: BMW F 450 R Expected Price, Launch Date November 2026 | ZigWheels (part 10)

## F 450 R Key Highlights

**Features:**
The BMW F 450 R gets a 6.5-inch TFT display with connected features such as navigation, music controls and call/SMS alerts. It also gets LED lighting, a USB-C charging port and heated grips.
The bike comes with Rain, Road and Dynamic riding modes, which alter the power delivery and how the bike responds to rider inputs. The M Sport variants get Riding Modes Pro with an additional Dynamic Pro mode. Other electronic features include Dynamic Traction Control (DTC), Engine Drag Torque Control (MSR) and switchable dual-channel ABS.
The optional Easy Ride Clutch (ERC) can automatically operate the clutch depending on engine speed, while the reversible gear lever can be switched to a GP shift pattern for track riding.

**Engine:**
The BMW F 450 R is powered by a 420 cc parallel-twin engine making 48 PS at 8,750 rpm and 43 Nm at 6,750 rpm. The motor is paired to a six-speed gearbox. The bike gets a bidirectional quickshifter on the higher variants.

page_chunks.title: BMW F 450 R Expected Price, Launch Date November 2026 | ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## F 450 R Key Highlights

**Suspension, Brakes & Other Details:**
Suspension duties are handled by a 43mm KYB inverted fork at the front and a KYB monoshock mounted to an aluminium double-sided swingarm at the rear. The optional Sport Suspension adds full adjustability to the fork, while the rear shock gets adjustable preload and rebound damping.
The motorcycle rolls on 17-inch cast-aluminium alloy wheels, shod with 110-section front and 150-section rear tyres. Braking hardware includes a 310mm front disc with a Brembo four-piston caliper and a 240mm rear disc with a ByBre single-piston caliper.
The standard seat height is 790 mm. BMW will also offer optional seats that can lower the riding position by 15mm or raise it by 20mm.

**Rivals:**
The BMW F 450 R will rival the Aprilia Tuono 457 and KTM 390 Duke R in India.

## Latest Updates on Himalayan 750

Sep 5, 2026 : Royal Enfield showcased the Himalayan 750 at its Himalayan Basecamp in Leh, Ladakh, a day after launching the Himalayan 440. The bike shown was the road-biased version on alloy wheels.

The Royal Enfield Himalayan 750 has been spotted testing yet again, and this time, the images are by far the clearest ones. The road-biased variant was spotted, complete with alloy wheels at both ends, likely a 19-17-inch front/rear combo.

Key aspects that we can observe include an adjustable Showa fork, linked monoshock, Husvarna Norden 901-like bodywork that also somehow looks the part of a beefier Himalayan, upright riding stance, and plenty of ground clearance with a high-set side-slung 2-1 exhaust. The chassis is of course, all-new, with a fixed subframe that should be able to handle much better loads when it comes to luggage options.

The powerplant is likely to be a heavily modified, bored-out version of the 650 twin, likely producing around 55PS and 60Nm. The bike gets Bybre rotors with twin discs up front and a disc at the rear. We’re sure Royal Enfield will offer switchable ABS, hopefully with cornering functionality. ## Dragster 300 Key Highlights

**Suspension, Brakes & Other Details:**
The Italjet Dragster 300's biggest highlight is its Independent Steering System (ISS), which uses a hub-centre steering arrangement instead of a conventional telescopic fork. This system separates steering inputs from suspension movements, helping minimise front-end dive under hard braking and maintain consistent steering geometry during deceleration.
The front wheel is held by a single-sided forged aluminium swingarm, which is mounted low on the chassis. Its sculpted design leaves the right side of the front wheel exposed, highlighting the disc brake and multi-piece hub assembly.
The scooter also gets an adjustable, horizontally mounted central monoshock tucked inside the chassis tunnel.

## Overview

**Sporty Scoot for the Youth**

- The TVS NTorq 125 is the Chennai-based manufacturer's most powerful scooter.
- It is also one of our favourite 125cc scooters, in terms of performance.
- It comes in 6 different variants with a range of colours including Marvel Avengers-themed ones.

page_chunks.title: TVS NTORQ 125 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Sharp Lines**

- The TVS NTorq 125 looks really cool with its aggressive and sporty design. It comes with stylish body panels and is available in 14 different colours.
- It also has Marvel Avengers-themed graphics, including Spiderman, Thor, Captain America and Black Panther.
- Aggressive design might not appeal to more mature buyers

page_chunks.title: TVS NTORQ 125 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**Peppy Performance**

- The NTorq 125 gets a 124.8cc, air-cooled, single-cylinder engine which produces 9.38PS and 10.6Nm.
- It delivers an impressive performance for a 125cc scooter.
- The Race XP variant makes 10.2PS and 10.9Nm - making it India’s most powerful 125cc scooter.
- Race XP variant gets 2 riding modes - Race & Street - for better performance & mileage respectively
- The NTorq 125 Race XP accelerates from 0 to 60kmph in just 8.07 seconds.
- The engine feels at home at highway speeds of 70-80kmph as well.
- It delivers an impressive real-world mileage of about 51-54kmpl in the city and 55-56kmpl on the highway
- If you ride hard, the mileage figure tends to drop rapidly,

page_chunks.title: TVS NTORQ 125 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Ride Quality

**Sporty stiff, but pleasant**

- Ride quality is good on well-paved roads, thanks to its telescopic fork and monoshock.
- The 125cc scooter remains stable even at higher speeds.
- It has a 155mm ground clearance, so clearing speed breakers isn't an issue.
- The ride does feel stiff on broken roads, so you need to slow down for large bumps & potholes

page_chunks.title: TVS NTORQ 125 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**Handles as sharp as it looks**

- The TVS NTorq 125 offers sharp handling, thanks to its chunky 12-inch wheels.
- The scooter is very stable around the corners at high speeds, even with a pillion.
- It is pretty agile and can filter through traffic very easily.
- Although braking power is decent, the brakes lack feel, making precise braking difficult.

page_chunks.title: TVS NTORQ 125 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort & Storage

**Reasonably practical**

- The TVS NTorq 125 has a well-padded and slightly sloping single-piece seat, which is spacious for both rider and pillion
- It has a spacious footboard and easy-to-reach handlebar, providing an upright riding posture.
- Even if you're tall, you can sit comfortably with slightly bent elbows, keeping a straight posture.
- The soft seat feels good for short commutes, but can get painful over longer distances as you sink into it.
- Although the handlebar is tall, it might still foul with your knees while taking U-turns if you're very tall.

page_chunks.title: TVS NTORQ 125 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

**Packed to the gills**

- The NTorq gets a digital instrument console as standard with smartphone connectivity and turn-by-turn navigation.
- It even has cool features like a timer for 0-60kmph acceleration and a lap timer with top speed recording.
- You can also check after your ride things like distance, time, engine RPM, and average speed on the Race XP variant.
- All the variants get voice assistance as well, making it easy to switch riding modes and activate navigation.
- Voice assistance feature needs a phone headset, and is a bit finicky
- Although it has an external fuel filler cap, you need to take the key out of the ignition to open it

page_chunks.title: TVS NTORQ 125 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Youth appeal**

- The TVS NTorq 125 is the most powerful scooter in the 125cc category.
- It comes with handy riding modes and connects to Bluetooth through its app, giving you a bunch of features.
- It delivers good mileage and handles well, making it almost the perfect sporty scooter.
- Whether you're using it daily or for weekend rides, the NTorq 125 is one of the best 125cc scooters to consider.
- That said, it is a bit on the pricier side, especially if you want the more powerful/feature-packed variants.

page_chunks.content:

**Good Things**

- Best-in-class performance for a 125cc scooter

- Brakes could have been better, Higher-end variants are costly

If you want a fast, fun and well-equipped scooter, the TVS Ntorq 125 is a great pick. It continues to set the standard for performance in its category, and its sporty look makes it even more attractive. The only downside is its cost, mostly on the higher-end variants.

page_chunks.content:
## Overview

**Truly “Accessible”?**

- The Suzuki eAccess is the Japanese auto giant’s first electric scooter for the Indian market.
- We had first seen it at Auto Expo 2025, and recently we finally rode it.
- For context though, we’ve only ridden this e-scooter on a go-kart track, so we won’t be able to give you feel for how it is like to ride in real-world conditions
- Also, at the time of writing this review, Suzuki hasn’t announced prices for the eAccess, so how it stacks up against other e-scooters in the Indian market remains to be seen

page_chunks.title: Suzuki e Access  Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 21)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Old school sporty**

- The eAccess looks almost nothing like the Access 125, and has a distinct sporty flair
- The sloping front apron with the integrated turn indicators and the rectangular handlebar mounted LED headlight make it look like a sporty scooter from the 1990s, and that makes it feel really unique
- Both sets of LED turn indicators have a very distinct shape and look really great
- At the rear, the two-tone panels under the seat remind us a bit of the Hero Vida e-scooter
- The LED tail light has a very unique shape, which along with the rear turn indicators, makes the eAccess look really attractive from the rear
- We particularly loved the design of diamond cut alloy wheels, particularly on full display at the rear thanks to the single-sided swingarm.

page_chunks.title: Suzuki e Access  Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 22)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

These add a serious premium touch to the scooter’s design
- The long vertical LED strip on the middle of the front apron looks like a bit of an overkill in terms of design
- The bog-standard mirrors too don’t gel too well with the overall sweeping lines of the eAccess
- Some might find that eAccess looks a little too small (although it doesn’t feel small once you sit on it)

page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

- The eAccess feels reasonably quick up to about 50kmph, after which the performance starts tapering off. This should be adequate for most people when riding in the city
- If ridden normally, we believe that the eAccess should be able to manage a range of 75-80km on a full charge, which again should be enough for people who have a daily commute of about 30-40km.
- The throttle calibration on the eAccess feel particularly good, acceleration is smooth regardless how hard you open the throttle, and feels extremely predictable.
- The braking regeneration in Mode A and Eco is quite strong, and it’s actually possible to ride this scooter with minimum brakes in the city
- The best part is that no matter how hard you ride the eAccess, it does not derate performance until the battery’s SoC (State of Charge) reaches 10 percent
- The on-paper specs of the Suzuki eAccess aren’t that impressive
- With a 4.1kW mid-mounted motor the eAccess has a top speed of just 71kmph
- Even the claimed range of 9

page_chunks.title: Suzuki e Access  Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 25)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

5km on a full charge feels a bit lacking compared to other premium e-scooters in the market
- When riding the eAccess quickly on the go-kart track, we saw a range drop commensurate with about 0.5km per percent of battery charge. So that would mean, when ridden hard, you can expect only about 50km of range from the scooter.
- The “three” riding modes are a bit confusing - Mode A give you the full top speed of 71kmph with maximum regen, Mode B gives you the same top speed with the least regen and Eco gives you a limited top speed of 55kmph with maximum regen
- You can switch between Mode A and Eco, as well as Mode B and Eco on the fly. But to change from A to B requires you to come to a complete halt and hold down the mode button for a couple of seconds

**Easy Charging**

page_chunks.title: Suzuki e Access  Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 27)
page_chunks.content:
## Battery & Charging

- The home charger is very well designed and has its own neat carrying bag, so that it won’t rattle around in the boot when you’re carrying it with you.
- Suzuki does offer fast charging with the eAccess, which can charge the battery from 0 to 100 percent in 2 hours and 12 minutes
- Suzuki also says that they will have fast charger available at most of their larger dealerships in 30 cities quite soon, with other cities and town following shortly
- Suzuki decided to go with an LFP (Lithium Ferro Phosphate) battery for the eAccess in order to give it a much longer battery life compared to other battery chemistries.
- The 3.07kWh battery pack is a bit small compared to its competition, and only offer a max claimed range of 95km on a full charge
- Home charging times are a bit on the higher side - 0 to 100 percent takes 6 hours and 20 minutes
- The LFP battery chemistry means the charge density is a bit lower compared to NMC (Nickle Manganese Cobalt) batteries, which makes the eAccess’ bat

page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**Quick footed**

- The eAccess is a nimble handler, and very eager to change direction
- At the same time, once it’s leaned over, it feels really stable - something we experienced and enjoyed on our ride on the go-kart track
- The brakes feel good too, with the front disc brake giving precise stopping power whenever you need it
- Even though the eAccess has a combined braking system, it’s still too easy to lock up the rear wheel if you just use the rear brake lever

page_chunks.title: Suzuki e Access  Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 30)
page_chunks.content:
## Ride Quality

**Meant for the family**

- We couldn’t thoroughly test the eAccess’ ride quality as we only rode on a go-kart track.
- But over the few plastic speedbreakers which were placed on the track, the front telescopic suspension felt quite well settled
- The rear suspension felt quite firm on those speedbreakers, and would bounce you around if you rode over them too quickly.
- We believe that the rear ride quality should become better with a pillion on board

page_chunks.title: Suzuki e Access  Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 31)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort & Storage

**The big easy**

- The eAccess’ seat is quite large and can accommodate a large rider as well as a large pillion quite comfortably
- With a seat height of just 765mm, it’s quite easy for riders of most heights to get both their feet on the gound
- The seat cushioning too is slightly on the firmer side, which we think should make it great for longer commutes
- The floorboard also runs up the apron in the same way as the Burgman, so riders can plant their feet forward, like on a cruiser, and get comfortable that way.
- The floorboard space is a bit lacking if you want to carry a large backpack on it
- Even the underseat storage is quite underwhelming, and might barely fit a single half face helmet, or a few groceries.

page_chunks.title: Suzuki e Access  Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 32)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

**Built Basic**

- The 4.2 inch colour TFT screen is very easy to read and legible even under harsh sunlight
- It also gets connectivity features such as Turn-by-turn navigation, weather alerts and call & message alerts
- The most unique feature the eAccess offers is its seat, which stays up once you open it. And to close it, you just lift it further to undo its retaining mechanism, and down it comes
- Reverse mode is a useful feature it gets
- We couldn’t test any of the connected features as the Suzuki Ride Connect app doesn’t list the eAccess as of yet
- Reverse mode is a bit fidgety to access - at a standstill, you need to hold the brake and push the power button for a couple of seconds, and then you need to turn the throttle in the opposite direction to move the scooter backwards.

page_chunks.title: Suzuki e Access  Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 33)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Should you buy the Suzuki eAccess?**

- At this point, it’s a bit difficult to recommend the eAccess as prices aren’t out yet. In fact, a lot rides on the pricing of this eAccess. If Suzuki can keep the price at Rs 1.10 lakh of below, the eAccess might make sense as it offers decent performance, acceptable range and top-notch build quality and fit-and-finish
- However, if the price goes above Rs 1.10 lakh (ex-showroom), it might be very difficult to justify the eAccess, especially compared to some of the other premium eScooters in the Indian market

## Overview

**A Fun, Family-Oriented, Eco-Friendly Commuter**

- The TVS iQube is a family-oriented electric scooter which has a simple, minimalistic design language, quite a bit of features and a decent range
- The base variant is available in two battery pack variants: 2.2kWh and 3.4kWh
- The new iQube MillionR Special Edition celebrates one million customers and is based on the 3.5kWh variant
- It gets a claimed 145km IDC (Indian Driving Conditions) range, Aurora Green Dual Tone colour, MillionR badging, new graphics, apron-mounted glovebox, and a USB Type-C port

page_chunks.title: TVS iQube Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Simple Yet Elegant**

- The scooter has a very simple and elegant design language
- The slim LED headlight with integrated indicators and the conventional family scooter design make it appealing to a wide range of audience
- The design is mundane which does not allow the scooter to stand out
- Switch gear quality could have been better

page_chunks.title: TVS iQube Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**Surprising Good**

- The scooter is deceivingly quick when compared to its petrol-powered counterparts
- Even the Eco mode is quite useable despite being capped at a lower top speed
- The Power mode is very responsive and propels the scooter to a claimed top-speed of 78kmph
- Regen works well too, and allows the scooter to slow down without needing to use the brakes
- The claimed range of 75km on a full charge should be enough for most people
- Regen only activates once the range drops down to 65km
- Top speed could have been better

page_chunks.title: TVS iQube Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**Heavy Yet Agile**

- The battery pack’s weight is well-distributed which makes the scooter light on its feet and quite agile
- The disc brake up front and a drum at the rear offer good braking performance, better than its ICE counterparts
- The scooter is on the heavier side which means that moving in and around the parking lot is a bit cumbersome

page_chunks.title: TVS iQube Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Ride Quality

**Best Of Both Worlds**

- The suspension does a decent job of absorbing bumps and undulations
- While the rear suspension is a bit firm, the ride quality gets better with a pillion
- The rear shock absorbers are set on the firmer side and may toss you off the seat on sharper bumps

page_chunks.title: TVS iQube Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 16)
page_chunks.content:

**More Than You Think**

- The 770mm tall seat is accessible for most average-sized riders
- It is long, wide and well-padded for a single rider as well as a pillion
- The floorboard & underseat storage facility are commendable, and enough for most
- Misses out on a four-in-one combi-lock system to remotely access the seat
- Does not get an apron-mounted phone holder
- USB charging port is located underneath the seat

page_chunks.title: TVS iQube Price November 2026 - Range, Charging Time, Colours | ZigWheels (part 17)

- The TFT display is very crisp and offers a lot of useful information at a single glance

## Overview

**Overview**

- The Hero Vida VX2 is Hero MotoCorp's latest offering in the electric scooter segment, designed for urban commuters looking for practicality, affordability, and smart features. It is available in two variants; VX2 Go and VX2 Plus. The VX2 Go variant has 3 sub variants: 3.4kWh, 2.2 kWh RQ and 2.2kWh. And the Plus variant also has 2 sub-variants– 4.4kWh and 3.4kWh.The scooter stands out with its unique Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS) model, which lowers the initial cost of ownership. The VX2 aims to provide a modern EV experience at a competitive price point. While it may not be the most premium or high-performance e-scooter on the market, the VX2 strikes a good balance between functionality and value, making it a choice to consider for everyday city use.

- You can easily ride at city speeds in 3rd gear. But above 55kmph in 3rd, the vibrations get a bit prominent
- On highways, the Ronin starts to struggle at higher speeds, with vibrations creeping in above 80kmph
- The bike lacks top-end performance, limiting its potential for long-distance cruising compared to models like the Apache RTR 200 4V

page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**Quick-footed**

- Despite its relaxed rake angle, the Ronin remains agile, thanks to its wide handlebar and manageable 160kg kerb weight
- The bike is easy to manoeuvre in the city due to its low seat height
- The block-pattern tyres provide good grip, even when cornering at higher speeds, enhancing confidence on twisty roads
- Braking performance could be better, with the lever feeling spongy and lacking proper feedback during hard braking situations

page_chunks.content:
## Ride Quality

**Well-tuned**

- The upright riding posture adds to rider comfort, while the bike’s suspension is well-tuned for city use, absorbing bumps and rough roads
- The bike handles rough terrain with ease, while still offering stability at higher speeds

page_chunks.title: TVS Ronin Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort & Storage

**Like a Cruiser**

- Low seat allows shorter rides to get their feet down easily
- Comfortable and upright riding posture
- Forward set footpegs and handlebar gives it an almost cruiser-like riding position
- Features, like a heel-toe shifter, could make longer rides even more comfortable
- The forward-set footpeg position can feel awkward for taller riders, especially when manoeuvring in tight spaces

page_chunks.title: TVS Ronin Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

**Feature-packed**

- The Ronin features a compact LCD screen with smartphone connectivity through TVS SmartXonnect, available on the higher-end TD variant
- The TVS SmartXonnect allows access to features such as call and SMS alerts, navigation, and phone battery status
- The silent starter operates smoothly, adding convenience, while the engine kill switch is a useful safety addition
- The small LCD screen tends to be cluttered with information, making it difficult to read while riding

page_chunks.title: TVS Ronin Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Is the TVS Ronin worth it?**

- The TVS Ronin is a well-equipped, urban-centric bike that excels in city commuting with its strong low-end torque and impressive manoeuvrability
- Lacks top-end performance and the mixed-bag design might not appeal to everyone
- Priced higher than other TVS models, such as the Apache RTR 160 4V and the NTorq 125, the Ronin leaves room for improvement, particularly in terms of refinement and long-distance comfort
- If utility and urban riding are your top priorities, the Ronin is a solid choice, but it may fall short for those seeking a ‘special’ riding experience

page_chunks.title: TVS Ronin Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Ronin Pros and Cons

**Good Things**

- Torquey engine ensures you don’t have to shift as frequently
- Excellent fit and finish
- Lightweight and agile in both city traffic and highway
- Can easily accommodate tall riders

**Could be Better**

- Unimpressive highway performance
- You’ll need to pull the front brake lever really hard for aggressive braking

**Expert's Conclusion**

The confusing styling aside, the Ronin is still a peppy and friendly motorcycle that is good for everyday commutes. The engineering finesse and build quality is decent but the styling and top-end engine performance isn’t. The Ronin also comes off as a bit expensive for a bike that is primarily meant to be a city commuter.

## Rebel 300 Key Highlights

**Price:**
The Honda Rebel 300 has been launched in India. It’s the brand’s smallest cruiser in the country, priced at Rs 2,22,000 for the Standard version, and Rs 2,62,000 for the one with the E-Clutch, both ex-showroom Bengaluru.

**Design:**
The India-made Rebel 300 looks similar to the one sold abroad. It’s got a minimalistic bobber-themed design with fat tyres at both ends, chopped fenders, and simple bodywork along with a swooping peanut tank. All in all, it looks like part of a factory custom.

**Features:**
The motorcycle comes equipped with a TFT console with smartphone connectivity and turn-by-turn navigation. It also gets an all-LED lighting setup with a projector headlight, dual-channel ABS, and Honda's E-Clutch technology, which allows riders to start, stop, and shift gears without operating the clutch lever. Of course, it also gives riders the option to use the clutch manually.

page_chunks.title: Honda Rebel 300 Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Rebel 300 Key Highlights

**Engine:**
The Honda Rebel 300 E-Clutch is powered by a 286cc, liquid-cooled engine. While the output figures of the India-spec version are not revealed yet, the one sold abroad makes 30.4PS and 27.4Nm, so expect the figures to be in the same ballpark. It is linked to a 6-speed gearbox.

**Suspension, Brakes & Other Details:**
The Rebel 300 is built on a tubular steel frame and gets a 41mm telescopic front fork along with twin rear shock absorbers. The bike gets disc brakes both for front and rear with dual-channel ABS.

**Rivals:**
The Honda Rebel 300 E-Clutch goes up against the Royal Enfield Meteor 350, Royal Enfield Goan Classic 350, Jawa 42 Bobber, Jawa Perak, and Yezdi Roadster. However, it will stand out by offering Honda's unique E-Clutch technology, which is currently unavailable in the segment.

## Overview

**The New King Of The Hill**

- The 2025 KTM 390 Adventure is built on the same platform as the Gen 3 390 Duke
- The bike gets adjustable long-travel suspension at both ends and has riding characteristics which leaps and bounds ahead of any motorcycle in the same segment
- KTM Adventure 390 S has become expensive by Rs 8,107 and comes at the price of Rs 4,04,851 (ex-showroom Delhi, as of July 2026).

page_chunks.title: KTM 390 Adventure S Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 23)
page_chunks.content:
## Design

**Dakar Inspired**

- Gets a very purposeful Dakar rally bikes inspired design
- The dual-LED projector headlights, the high-mounted beak, long single-piece seat and the narrow tail section gel well together and complete the overall design
- The design might not appeal to everyone as it is very polarizing

page_chunks.title: KTM 390 Adventure S Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 24)
page_chunks.content:
## Performance & Mileage

**Best-in-class**

- The engine is very tractable when going offroad, at city speeds and even when doing highway speeds
- The larger rear sprocket over the 390 Duke means that it has better low-end response
- The motorcycle is very quick and has a claimed 0-100kmph time of 6.17 seconds
- The bidirectional quickshifter is super slick and allows you to change gears rapidly
- You will feel vibrations creeping in the footpegs when you go over 6,000rpm

page_chunks.title: KTM 390 Adventure S Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 25)
page_chunks.content:
## Handling

**A sportsbike in disguise**

- The bike is always ready to change directions on a dime
- The long wheelbase and Apollo Tramplr tyres makes it very stable when it is leaned over
- Brakes are powerful enough to stop the adventure bike quickly
- The axial brake caliper does not provide an instant bite which we feel on the 390 Duke

page_chunks.title: KTM 390 Adventure S Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 26)
page_chunks.content:
## Ride Quality

**Built for all-roads**

- The adjustable suspension at both ends means that the ride quality can be customised to the required usage
- The suspension absorbs all bumps and potholes very easily giving you a riding experience like no other motorcycle
- Even after going through sharp bumps, the bike never feels unsettled and goes through everything
- The stock suspension setup may feel a bit stiff if you are on the lighter side, though, it can be adjusted

page_chunks.title: KTM 390 Adventure S Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 27)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort & Storage

**An excellent tourer**

- The riding posture is very comfortable and provides you an upright posture
- Even when going offroad, the slim mid-section of the seat means that it is easy to grip the bike with your legs and get in a good attack position
- The light kerb weight and low seat height allows the rider to pick the bike up easily and maneuver in the parking lot without breaking a sweat
- The seat height may feel a bit short for riders above 6 feet
- The seat is a bit narrow and firm which will affect your daily city commuting experience

## Features

**Loaded to the brim**

- Gets a 5-inch TFT display with riding modes and smartphone connectivity
- Rider aids include cornering ABS and cornering traction control
- Gets cruise control as standard which is very helpful while touring

page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

**Should you buy the KTM 390 Adventure?**

- The 390 Adventure is a motorcycle which you cannot ignore no matter what
- The performance it offers, the features it gets and the equipment it has is unparalleled by any other motorcycle in the segment
- Though priced a bit on the higher side, the 390 Adventure is an excellent value for money proposition

page_chunks.title: KTM 390 Adventure S Price, Mileage & Colours | ZigWheels (part 30)
page_chunks.content:
## 390 Adventure S Pros and Cons

**Good Things**

- Feels incredibly light and easy to manage
- Tubeless spoke wheels are a real boon for handling punctures
- Motor is tractable, making it easy to ride in the city or even off road
- Cruise control works great when touring on highways
- Nearly fully-adjustable suspension lets you set the bike up for your weight or riding style easily
- Fantastic highway performance
- No wind buffeting at over 100kmph

**Could be Better**

- Slight vibrations in the footpegs above 6000rpm
- Need to remove a side panel to adjust rear preload setting
- Footpeg rubbers need a spanner to remove

**Expert's Conclusion**

The KTM 390 Adventure with the 2025 update has undergone a massive overhaul both in terms of looks, features and performance. But the pricing when compared to its segment rivals is a bit too high. The bike overall is more geared towards hardcore offroaders.

Royal Enfield Himalayan 750 Review: Is This The ULTIMATE ADV Under...

- Nov 15, 2026
- Views : 99

The Royal Enfield Himalayan 750 recently made its global debut around EICMA 2026. The big ADV is the first bike from the brand’s 750cc platform, and is quite well equipped - in terms of performance as well as features.

The ADV will be launched in India at the Motoverse festival in Goa, from November 27 to 29. If you are awaiting its launch to buy the bike, here’s 5 key things you need to know about the Royal Enfield Himalayan 750.

The Himalayan 750 is powered by a new 750cc twin-cylinder engine that makes 55PS and 63Nm. That allows the bike to sustain triple digit highway speeds without breaking a sweat. That means touring on the new Himalayan is a breeze.

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Himalayan 750 Reviewed: Top 5 Pros & Cons  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
On the flip side, urban riding is quite good too. It has a strong low-end performance that should help make it easy to ride in our urban stop-go traffic conditions. You can move around at lower revs, and should you need a quick burst for overtake, just open the throttle more.

Once astride the bike, you’ll realise that it has a roomy cockpit, and comfortable ergonomics. It is definitely one of the roomiest bikes in its class. That said, won’t stretch you out. Everything is well within reach and the bike feels comfortable whether you are commuting or out on a long-distance tour. The well-padded seat makes it genuinely very comfortable for mile-munching.

That said, despite its 815mm tall seat, anyone taller than 5 feet 5 inches should be able to easily swing a leg over the seat. For even taller riders, there’s an optional seat that increases the height by 20mm. But shorter riders fret not, the lower seat drops the stock height by 20mm.

page_chunks.title: Royal Enfield Himalayan 750 Reviewed: Top 5 Pros & Cons  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
The Himalayan 750 might look quite big and bulky, but appearances can be deceiving. Despite its visual heft, the ADV feels effortless in changing directions. This while feeling quite planted out on the highway.

As nimble as the Himalayan may feel, there’s no ignoring the fact that it weighs 224kg kerb. While it may feel light on the move, parking the bike or moving it at slow speeds will make you feel its weight. That said, once you get a hang of it, life should be easier.

The Himalayan is quite a tech-laden bike, which is why the lack of a quickshifter sticks out like a sore thumb. While the gearbox is slick, a quickshifter should at least have been offered as an accessory. More than for the sportiness of it, it would have made touring an even easier affair.
