## Family Trips, Big Luggage, Long Miles And Wild Detours: Why The Mahindra Scorpio-N Is The Complete Family SUV

- Published November 10, 2026
- Views : 1468
- 11 min read

Indian family trips rarely go to plan. You set out for a quiet weekend getaway, and suddenly the cousins are coming too. The grandparents need the comfortable seats, the kids want the windows, and someone has packed three bags “just in case.” Before you know it, the car isn’t carrying four people. It’s carrying six, plus luggage, snacks, a cooler box and a pram, on a 500 km drive that ends on a dirt road.

That’s a lot to ask of any car. It’s also exactly what Mahindra SUVs have been doing for generations. They’ve been the go-to for wedding trips, temple visits and long drives back to the hometown, and they keep going where the road gets rough.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## Family Trips, Big Luggage, Long Miles And Wild Detours: Why The Mahindra Scorpio-N Is The Complete Family SUV

The Scorpio-N carries that tradition forward. It covers all of a family’s needs: space for everyone, room for everything, comfort for long hours on the road, highway stamina, and the 4x4 ability to turn a regular trip into an adventure.

So how does it handle real family life? We looked past the brochure photos at the space, luggage capacity, comfort, long-distance ability and off-road skill that matter most when the whole family is on board.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## Made For Family Trips: Space For Everyone

A great family trip starts with everyone fitting in comfortably, and that starts with size. The Scorpio-N has plenty of it. Its large exterior dimensions give it room for three proper rows inside, and the numbers explain why it feels so roomy the moment you step in.

| **Dimension** | **Measurement** |
| Length | 4662 mm |
| Width | 1917 mm |
| Height | 1857 mm (without ski rack and antenna) |
| Wheelbase | 2750 mm |

What it means for your family:

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## Made For Family Trips: Space For Everyone

- Wheelbase (2750 mm): This is the distance between the front and rear wheels, and it decides how much room there is between the seats. A long wheelbase like the Scorpio-N’s is what makes room for three rows.
- Width (1917 mm): More width means more shoulder room, especially in the second row. Three people can sit side by side without fighting over the armrests.
- Height (1857 mm): A tall cabin gives generous headroom and an airy feel. Everyone gets a high view out of the windows, which keeps kids entertained and helps passengers who get carsick.
- Length (4662 mm): It’s long enough for three rows and a usable boot, but still manageable in city traffic.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
## Six Or Seven Seats: Your Family, Your Layout

Every family is different, so the Scorpio-N offers two seating layouts.

The 7-seater is offered across the range, from the base Z2 to the top Z8L. It’s the layout for families who regularly need every seat.

- First row: Two front seats with a high, commanding driving position.
- Second row: A three-seat bench, ideal for parents with two kids, or three adults on a city run.
- Third row: Two more seats, well suited to children and shorter trips. They fold away when you need luggage space instead.

The 6-seater is offered on the top Z8L. It’s the layout for families who put comfort ahead of seat count.

- Second-row captain seats: Two individual seats replace the bench, so each passenger gets their own space. Older parents will especially appreciate this on long journeys.
- Easier third-row access: The gap between the captain seats creates a walkway to the back row, so no one has to fold or tumble a seat to get in.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:
## Six Or Seven Seats: Your Family, Your Layout

Which one suits you? If you often carry six or seven people, or have young kids who’ll use the third row, go for the 7-seater. If the third row is only for occasional use and you want more comfort for older parents, the 6-seater makes long drives more relaxed.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 7)
page_chunks.content:
## Flexible Seats For Changing Plans

Family plans change quickly, and the Scorpio-N’s seats keep up. They fold and move in a few simple steps, so you can switch between carrying people and carrying cargo in seconds.

- Second row, 1-touch tumble (left side): One pull, and the left section tumbles forward to open a path to the third row.
- Third row, fold and tumble: Fold it away to free up luggage space when it’s just five of you.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## Luggage: Pack Everything, Leave Nothing Behind

Every family knows the struggle of fitting the luggage in. There are suitcases, a stroller, a cooler box and the bag of snacks someone insisted on. The Scorpio-N makes this one of the easiest parts of the trip.

With the third row folded, you get 786 litres of boot space. That’s enough for most families’ biggest trips.

What 786 litres means in real life:

- Large suitcases for a week-long family holiday
- A folded pram, a cooler box and shopping bags, all at once
- Camping gear, sports kits or wedding luggage
- A tall loading area for bulky items that won’t fit in a smaller SUV

Smart loading touches:

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## Luggage: Pack Everything, Leave Nothing Behind

- Side-hinged tailgate: The tailgate swings open sideways like a door. You don’t need to reach up to pull it shut, which helps shorter family members. It also opens up the full width of the boot for loading bulky items.
- Roof-mounted ski rack: Mahindra’s name for its roof rails. You can add a roof carrier for extra luggage, camping equipment or bicycles on longer trips.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfort: Happy Passengers In Every Row

On a long drive, comfort matters as much as space. A cramped, hot cabin makes everyone grumpy. A cool, comfortable one with something to do in every row keeps the whole family happy. The Scorpio-N takes care of every passenger, from the driver to the kids in the back.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## Cool Cabin, Even In Peak Summer

Indian summers are tough, and in a three-row SUV the rear rows can warm up quickly. The Scorpio-N handles this from the base variant up.

- Second-row AC vents: Standard on every Scorpio-N.
- Rear AC blower: Rear passengers get their own blower control. Mahindra says the rear AC is designed to send air to every corner of the cabin.
- Dual-zone automatic climate control: The driver and front passenger can set their own temperatures.
- Ventilated front seats: These cool the seat surface itself, a relief after a hot day or a long stretch at the wheel.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Seats That Feel Good After Hours On The Road

- Seat height adjustment and lumbar support for the driver.
- 6-way powered driver seat: Find the right driving position at the press of a button.
- Coffee-black leatherette upholstery: From the Z8S onwards. It looks rich and wipes clean easily after spills, crumbs and muddy shoes. Lower variants get fabric seats.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Charging For Every Row

Every passenger on a family trip has a device to keep alive: a phone for navigation, a tablet for the kids, a portable game console. The Scorpio-N gives each row its own power source.

- First row: A wireless charging pad with active cooling on higher variants, plus a 65W USB Type-C fast-charging port for phones, tablets and even some laptops.
- Second row: USB Type-C charging ports, including a 65W port, so second-row passengers can charge their own devices.
- Third row: A 12V charging socket, standard on every variant.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 14)
page_chunks.content:
## Mile Muncher: Built For The Long Drive Home

For many Indian families, the most important trip of the year is the long drive back to the hometown. It might be 400 km, 800 km or more, often in one go. This is where the Scorpio-N really shines. It’s an SUV that covers long distances with ease, so everyone, including the driver, arrives fresh.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 15)
page_chunks.content:
## Strong Engines For Easy Highway Driving

|  | **2-litre turbo-petrol** | **2.2-litre diesel** |
| Power | 203 PS | Up to 175 PS |
| Torque | Up to 380 Nm | Up to 400 Nm |
| Transmission | 6-speed MT / 6-speed AT | 6-speed MT / 6-speed AT |

What it means on the highway:

- Effortless overtakes: The petrol’s 203 PS and the diesel’s strong torque mean you can pass slow trucks on two-lane highways without waiting for a huge gap.
- Relaxed even when fully loaded: The diesel’s torque arrives from low engine speeds, so a fully loaded Scorpio-N with seven people and their luggage still drives easily.
- Sixth gear for cruising: Both gearboxes have six speeds, which helps the engine stay relaxed at highway speeds.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 16)
page_chunks.content:
## A Smooth, Settled Ride

Indian highways aren’t always smooth, and a long drive on broken roads can tire everyone out. The Scorpio-N’s suspension is built to deal with that.

- Long 2750 mm wheelbase: Helps the SUV ride in a settled way at highway speeds.
- Frequency Dependent Damping (FDD): The shock absorbers respond differently to small, quick bumps than to big, slow movements. Road joints and rough patches feel softer, and the SUV stays composed over bigger potholes.
- Double wishbone front and pentalink rear with Watt’s linkage: This setup keeps the Scorpio-N stable and planted, even on uneven surfaces.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 17)
page_chunks.content:
## Safety: Peace Of Mind For Every Passenger

When your whole family is on board, safety comes first. Every Scorpio-N comes with the essentials, and higher variants add more.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 18)
page_chunks.content:
## Safety: Peace Of Mind For Every Passenger

- ISOFIX and i-SIZE child seat compatibility: On every variant, for safely securing child seats.
- 3-point seatbelts for all seats: Including the middle passenger in the second row and both third-row passengers.
- Seatbelt reminders for all seats: With an occupant detection system, so the driver knows if anyone hasn’t buckled up.
- Front seatbelt pretensioners: These tighten the front belts instantly in a collision.
- 6 Airbags: From the Z8S onwards, covering the front, side and curtain areas.
- Electronic stability control, ABS with EBD and all-wheel disc brakes: Standard on every variant.
- E-call and SOS button: In an emergency, press the SOS button, or let automatic crash detection take over. Either way, your location goes to Mahindra’s assistance service and your emergency contacts.
- Level 2 ADAS: On the Z8L, functions include autonomous emergency braking, which can detect vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 19)
page_chunks.content:
## Adventure: 4XPLOR Takes Your Family Further

This is where the Scorpio-N goes beyond being just a family SUV. Most family cars stop where the tarmac ends. The Scorpio-N 4x4 is built to keep going, and that opens up a whole new set of places for your family to discover.

Think of a riverside campsite at the end of a dirt track, or a beach you can only reach across soft sand. Picture a hill viewpoint up a rocky trail, a plantation stay down a rain-soaked road, or a snowy pass on a winter holiday. With most family cars, you look at these places from a distance. With a Scorpio-N 4x4, you can drive right up to them.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 20)
page_chunks.content:
## No Expertise Needed

You don’t need to be an expert off-roader to use any of this. 4XPLOR is designed so that a parent who has never driven off the road can still take the family down a muddy track to a campsite with confidence. The terrain modes do most of the thinking for you.

page_chunks.title: Mahindra Scorpio-N Space & Practicality: How Good Is It For Families?  - ZigWheels (part 21)
page_chunks.content:
## Your Camping Partner

The Scorpio-N’s practicality makes it a natural fit for camping:

- 786 litres of boot space (third row folded) for tents, sleeping bags, cooking gear and a cooler box
- Roof-mounted ski rack for a roof carrier with extra gear
- 12V socket in the third row to power a portable cooler or camping light
- 57-litre fuel tank for long stretches between fuel stations in remote areas
- Seats for up to seven, so the whole family or a group of friends can come along

page_chunks.content:
## Perfect For Family: How The Scorpio-N Ticks Every Box

So does the Scorpio-N meet everything a family needs? Here’s a quick look at how it handles each part of family life:

Buying your first family electric scooter can be a difficult decision to make. It should be practical, comfortable, and easy to live with every day. The Ampere Magnus GMax aims to tick all these boxes with features designed to make everyday riding easier, be it commuting to work, running errands, or dropping your kids off at school. Here are the top 5 reasons you should consider the Ampere scooter:

page_chunks.title: Ampere Magnus G Max: Savings, Storage & Convenience Pro Max  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## Practicality Pro Max

One of the biggest highlights of the Ampere Magnus GMax is its 33-litre underseat storage compartment. It offers plenty of space for everyday essentials such as groceries, helmets, and even your laptop bag.

It also has a spacious, flat floorboard to carry stuff, along with built-in luggage hooks where you can carry everyday shopping bags with ease. All of this makes the Ampere Magnus GMax a perfect companion for your everyday needs.

page_chunks.title: Ampere Magnus G Max: Savings, Storage & Convenience Pro Max  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## Comfortable For The Whole Family

The Ampere Magnus GMax is designed to be used by all members of your family. It has an accessible 800 mm seat height, which should make it comfortable for shorter riders too. The seat itself is pretty spacious, and the relaxed riding position makes it comfortable for everyday use.

The scooter gets 12-inch wheels at both ends and 165 mm of ground clearance, which should help it tackle bad roads with ease. It also weighs just 116 kg, making it light and easy to handle for everyone in your family.

page_chunks.title: Ampere Magnus G Max: Savings, Storage & Convenience Pro Max  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## Low Running Costs

Being an EV, the Ampere Magnus GMax will have lower running costs than a comparable ICE vehicle. It has a 3 kWh battery pack, which offers a claimed IDC (Indian Driving Cycle) range of 142 km, and you can expect a real-world range of over 100km. This means that, over time, the savings from its electric powertrain could help reduce everyday commuting expenses significantly.

page_chunks.title: Ampere Magnus G Max: Savings, Storage & Convenience Pro Max  - ZigWheels (part 5)

This should make it suitable for everyday city commutes, whether you're zipping in and out of gaps or navigating stop-and-go traffic.

The scooter also gets three riding modes, Eco,Power and Reverse, with Eco mode delivering smooth and linear performance, while Power mode is suited for spirited riding and quick acceleration. This makes the Magnus GMax a practical option for everyday commuting for all members of your family, with enough performance for everyday needs.

page_chunks.title: Ampere Magnus G Max: Savings, Storage & Convenience Pro Max  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:

Priced at Rs 1.03 lakh (ex-showroom), the Ampere Magnus GMax is an affordable and practical family electric scooter built to tackle the urban environment. It has a long range, plenty of practical storage options, including 33-litre underseat storage and a large floorboard, making it perfect for urban duties.

So, if you are planning to buy a family electric scooter this festive season, the Ampere Magnus GMax is a solid option.

KTM unveiled the 1390 Super Duke GT Evo at EICMA 2026. The new motorcycle is a higher-spec version of the standard 1390 Super Duke GT and brings several upgrades, including an automated manual transmission (AMT), new semi-active suspension and an updated electronics package. The motorcycle is expected to reach international dealerships in early 2027.

Powering the KTM 1390 Super Duke GT Evo is a 1,350 cc, liquid-cooled, V-twin engine that produces 187 PS and 145 Nm. This is the same engine that also powers the 1390 Super Adventure S Evo. It is housed in a steel trellis frame and paired with a single-sided swingarm. One of the biggest highlights is the new AMT gearbox, which offers both fully automatic and manual shifting modes. This means riders can let the motorcycle handle gear changes or take control themselves whenever they want a more engaging riding experience.

page_chunks.title: 2027 KTM 1390 Super Duke GT EVO Unveiled  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content: The Super Duke GT Evo gets a new 48 mm WP Apex semi-active front fork with a patented thru-rod design, which is claimed to reduce weight and improve front-end feedback. At the rear, it gets a linked monoshock with electronically adjustable damping and hydraulic preload adjustment. The motorcycle also gets lighter 17-inch alloy wheels at both ends, reducing unsprung weight by 1.2 kg compared to the standard model. These are wrapped in Michelin Power 6 tyres.

page_chunks.title: 2027 KTM 1390 Super Duke GT EVO Unveiled  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
The motorcycle gets an extensive electronics package, including ride modes, traction control, a quickshifter and ABS. It also features an upgraded lighting setup with cornering lights, DRLs and a redesigned headlight. Another major highlight is the 8.8-inch TFT touchscreen display, which gets offline map navigation as standard. KTM has also made changes to the touring ergonomics with an adjustable windscreen, repositionable handlebar and redesigned rider and pillion seats. Braking duties are handled by Brembo Stylema four-piston front calipers with twin 320 mm discs, while the rear gets a two-piston caliper with a 240 mm disc.

The KTM 1390 Super Duke GT Evo is expected to go on sale internationally in early 2027, with availability varying across markets. KTM has previously brought its larger-capacity motorcycles, including the 1390 Super Duke R and 1290 Super Adventure S, to India. While the brand has not confirmed an India launch yet, the possibility cannot be ruled out.

page_chunks.content:
Has BMW Blown Every ADV Out Of The Park? F 450 GS Ridden In Goa

- Apr 26, 2026
- Views : 3520

BMW Motorrad **recently launched the much-awaited Sport variant of the F 450 GS in India**. It offers almost all the features of the top-spec Trophy variant without the ERC (Easy Ride Clutch) and at a slightly lower price of Rs 5.90 lakh (ex-showroom). However, that is still quite a premium for an adventure bike in the sub 500 cc category. The brand is also planning to bring the recently unveiled BMW F 450 R and F 450 RR to India by next year. Here’s what we expect them to cost.

When BMW first unveiled the F 450 R and F 450 RR, we expected the streetfighter to be priced at around Rs 4.60 lakh, while the fully-faired RR was expected to cost Rs 4.75 lakh (both ex-showroom). However, things have changed since then, and both motorcycles are now expected to arrive with considerably higher price tags.

page_chunks.title: Upcoming BMW F 450 R & F 450 RR: Expected Pricing In India  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
The BMW F 450 R could be priced at around Rs 5 lakh, while the F 450 RR is expected to cost approximately Rs 5.20 lakh (both ex-showroom). The new expected pricing has been assumed as per the current pricing of the F 450 GS, as the F 450 R and F 450 RR are based on this adventure bike. This also means that their top-spec variants could easily touch the Rs 6 lakh mark, considering that the F 450 GS Trophy currently costs Rs 6.15 lakh (ex-showroom).

For context, the Aprilia Tuono 457 is priced at Rs 3.99 lakh, while the fully-faired RS 457 costs Rs 4.26 lakh (both ex-showroom). This gives the Italian motorcycles a considerable price advantage even before the BMWs arrive.

Another interesting fact is that the German brand will be manufacturing these new bikes in India. Considering this, we hope the brand keeps the pricing competitive rather than positioning these motorcycles at a significant premium over their Italian rivals.

page_chunks.title: Upcoming BMW F 450 R & F 450 RR: Expected Pricing In India  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
We also hope BMW introduces the non-ERC variants of both motorcycles right from the beginning, instead of bringing them to India several months after the initial launch. This would give buyers more affordable options and make the F 450 R and F 450 RR more accessible. Ultimately, BMW has some interesting motorcycles coming to India, but their pricing will play a crucial role in determining how well they compete against the Aprilia 457 twins.

The Viaterra Holeshot Pro has been my go-to riding gloves for everything from daily commutes to weekend trips and trail rides. Over the past year, I’ve used them in virtually all riding scenarios, and recently, even witnessed an unexpected crash. Here’s how my experience with these gloves has been over this time period.

After extensive use, the gloves have stood the test of time. The stitching still remains tight. The mesh panels have remained in place except for a few threads here and there that got stuck in velcro, coming off.

The goat skin leather around the palm has begun creasing, but this is expected after near continuous daily use. Lastly, the velcro straps still clasp rather well. The only issues I’ve noticed are that the silicone grips on the palms have started to wear away.

Also, the colouring has begun fading. However, these are just minor issues, not deal-breakers, and the gloves have held up fantastically so far.

When we usually speak of protection, we usually talk about what the gloves offer on paper and rarely do we ever get an opportunity to test them out in the real world ourselves (not that we want to!). During a local race, I ended up getting one such opportunity due to an unexpected crash.

I participated in a local off-road rally with TeamRPM Pune. The race was divided into 2 stages, with each stage being 4km. During the first stage, almost everything went well, but at the end, I had a crash while taking a right turn.

page_chunks.content:
Touring On The Royal Enfield Himalayan 450: 5 Things I Learnt

- Dec 19, 2024
- Views : 3169

Tyres are the only contact points between a motorcycle and the road, well, unless you crash, which makes them far more important than most riders give them credit for. So when Eurogrip sent us the Trailhound SCR tyres, we knew it was time to see how they perform in different conditions. I’ve now shod my KTM 390 Adventure X with a set of Trailhound SCRs, kicking off what will be a long-term test to see how well these dual-purpose tyres hold up over everyday riding, touring, and light trail duty.

The Eurogrip Trailhound SCR is positioned as an on/off-road tyre for adventure and scrambler-style motorcycles. It’s designed to handle a mix of tarmac and mild off-road conditions, think gravel, hard-packed dirt, or broken roads, without compromising road stability.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip Trailhound SCR Tyres Long Term Review: First Impressions  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
The SCR uses a block-pattern tread for traction on loose surfaces and has a rounded profile for predictable cornering. They are priced at Rs 4,216 for the front (100/90-19) and Rs 7,269 for the rear (130/80 R17), which makes them among the more affordable dual-purpose options available in the market.

Eurogrip offers the Trailhound SCR in several popular ADV and scrambler sizes. These tyres are suitable for bikes like the Royal Enfield Himalayan 450, Yezdi Adventure, Suzuki V-Strom 250 SX, BMW G 310 GS, Triumph Scrambler 400X and other motorcycles. Essentially, motorcycles that spend most of their time on the road but still dabble in mild off-road exploration.

These are available in the factory-recommended sizes for the KTM 390 Adventure X. That means no changes to steering geometry or clearance, and the tyres sit perfectly within factory specifications.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip Trailhound SCR Tyres Long Term Review: First Impressions  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
Fitting them was a surprisingly straightforward job. The Trailhounds slipped onto the rims without much fuss, no bead-seating drama or balancing issues, and were ready to go after a quick alignment check. Visually, the Trailhounds look the part. The tread blocks are spaced evenly, and the overall profile gives the impression of a tyre which can handle all kinds of terrain.

The immediate difference I felt after the swap was that the bike now takes a bit more effort to steer, not heavy, but just enough to notice. On the flip side, grip over loose and gravely sections has noticeably improved, giving the front end more confidence and stability when the surface gets sketchy.

Over the next few months, I’ll be running the KTM 390 Adventure X on the Trailhound SCR tyres across a variety of conditions, from daily city commutes to long highway rides and some light trail runs.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip Trailhound SCR Tyres Long Term Review: First Impressions  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
I’ll be evaluating them on grip (both wet and dry), comfort, stability, noise levels, and wear patterns. Essentially, I want to find out if these tyres can strike that elusive balance between road comfort and trail confidence. For now, the installation was painless, the fit is spot on, and the first impressions are rather positive. Whether that remains true once the kilometres pile on, that’s what this long-term test will reveal.

## 2025 TVS YMRP Round 2: Finding My Footing

- Published September 14, 2025
- Views : 7878
- 3 min read

Fear is a strange companion. It lingers long after the moment has passed, showing up when you least expect it. For me, fear arrived in Round 1 of the TVS Young Media Race Program – the blinding flames of a burning bike, the violent hug of the airbag vest inflating and the huge deflation of my spirit. But thirteen weeks and another semi-eventful outing later, the evils of round 1 seemed to have been washed away.

page_chunks.title: Riding The TVS Apache RTR 200 4V Race-Spec Bike For TVS Young Media Racers Program Round 2  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## Gonna Fly Now

Fear has a way of fuelling determination. To shake it off, I started small with daily rides on empty stretches, pushing just enough to remind myself of the basics. And just a week before Round 2, the KTM 160 Duke we had at the office ended up being my secret weapon. Light, agile, precise and forgiving – the bike was one of the main reasons that helped stitch my confidence back together. By the time I left for Chennai for the second round, the fear hadn’t disappeared but rather I was ready to face it head-on.

page_chunks.title: Riding The TVS Apache RTR 200 4V Race-Spec Bike For TVS Young Media Racers Program Round 2  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## Practice Makes A Man Perfect?

The Madras International Circuit welcomed us with its usual cocktail of humidity and anticipation. My practice session started steady, but by the second lap something felt wrong. I clicked up for 5th gear: nothing. I tried again, still nothing. Worse, the bike bogged in 4th, leaving me stranded as riders sailed past, mocking my helpless throttle.

Frustrating? Absolutely. But this is where the TVS pit crew came in like quiet heroes. After the session, I rolled into the pits, explained what happened, and within minutes they were at work: tweaking, tightening, checking everything from the gearbox to tyre pressures. The funny thing is, the bike is set up for riders weighing 65-70 kg, and at 66 kilos, I fit right in. No special changes needed, except the crucial fix for the gearbox gremlin.

page_chunks.title: Riding The TVS Apache RTR 200 4V Race-Spec Bike For TVS Young Media Racers Program Round 2  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## Du du du du…..Max Verstappen

We had our qualifying session post launch, and the difference was night and day. The race-spec TVS Apache RTR 200 4V ran flawlessly, every shift clicking home with the precision I’d been missing. I felt lighter, faster, smoother. Proof? My lap times, from a time of 2:27.359 in practice, I shaved nearly three seconds off in qualifying for a best time of 2:24.912. Sure, I was still braking early, still hesitating into a few corners, but the improvement was real. Confidence, once broken, was slowly being rebuilt one lap at a time.

page_chunks.title: Riding The TVS Apache RTR 200 4V Race-Spec Bike For TVS Young Media Racers Program Round 2  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
## Nice Guys Finish Last

Race day dawned with the humid air thick with nervous energy. On the formation lap, everything felt normal. My grid slot was P12, and I knew I had work to do. Six laps stretched ahead of me. But as the lights went out, we launched, and déjà vu. The same gearbox issue that haunted my practice returned.

Power dipped, gears slipped, and all I could do was make the best of the situation at hand. Riders passed me in the corners, my lines felt messy, but I refused to give up. I kept it safe, steady, and above all, upright. By the chequered flag, I was still in 12th - the same place I started. Last? Definitely, but I was able to participate in the race this time.

page_chunks.title: Riding The TVS Apache RTR 200 4V Race-Spec Bike For TVS Young Media Racers Program Round 2  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:
## A Different Kind of Victory

Walking away from Round 2, I didn’t carry the **fear I had after Round 1**. I wasn’t haunted by flames or failure, instead I carried satisfaction. I had raced, I had finished, and I had felt joy again. For me round 2 wasn’t about trophies or lap records, it was about proving to myself that fear wouldn’t win twice.

Now, as I look ahead to Round 3, I’m not dreading it, I’m excited. For the first time since that crash, the track doesn’t feel like a place of danger. It feels like a challenge I can’t wait to take on.

page_chunks.content:
## Hero Xoom 160 First Ride Review: Worth The Wait?

- Published September 10, 2025
- Views : 8700
- 7 min read

Indian aspirations are on the rise. We want the latest, the funkiest, the most technologically superior, the most feature-packed products in every walk of life. And that same holds true when it comes to scooters because until now, we've looked up to 125 cc products as big. But then the Yamaha Aerox rolled in and that instantly became the benchmark for large, sporty, and meaningful scooters. So, when Hero showcased the Xoom 160 concept a couple of years ago and finally launched it earlier this year at the Auto Expo, there were a lot of expectations. It was a bold step from Hero. But it has been a long wait for the maxi-scooter to finally hit the Indian roads. And now that it is here, we had some critical questions that needed answering.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## IS IT ADVENTUROUS?

Don’t let the design language of the Xoom 160 fool you into thinking that it is some form of a soft-roader, or Hero’s scaled-down version of the Honda X-ADV 750. It is just a scooter that looks rugged but not capable enough of doing muddy stuff. It doesn’t have the foundations or the necessary hardware for it.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## IS IT SUBSTANTIAL?

Hero has played it big and bold when it comes to the styling of the Xoom 160. It claims the scooter has the company’s Dakar rally racer-inferences but I struggled to find the resemblance. It is still pretty impressive and imposing at the same time, making it quite unique in the Indian context, especially from an accessibility standpoint. It certainly feels substantial both when you look at it at standstill as well as from the saddle. Hence, giving you that maxi feel is what the Hero Xoom 160 does brilliantly.

What I wish Hero had made better is the quality of plastics used, particularly the matte black ones. They look a little cheap and can be easily prone to scratches. Overall, it has been put together rather well with nothing feeling rather flimsy.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## IS IT FUN?

|  | **Hero Xoom 160** |
| Engine | 156cc single, liquid-cooled |
| Power | 14.6PS at 8000rpm |
| Torque | 14Nm at 6500rpm |

The engine is a ground-up new design with a sense of liveliness packed into it. It isn’t the quickest or the raddest mills out there, taking a fair amount of time to reach speeds up to 65-70 kmph. It does feel noticeably quicker than the 125cc scooters in the market, though, which is exactly what you want from a scooter of this segment.

It will not beat the Yamaha Aerox in a drag race but it will keep pace with it on tours. There’s a certain amount of gruffness that you will appreciate as it toes the fine line between character and harshness. The throaty exhaust note adds to the sense of fun with the motor not feeling numb or lifeless.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
## IS IT FUN?

One must not forget that the Xoom 160 has a rather large mill and expecting scooter-like great fuel efficiency is not going to be possible. Hence, even though Hero claims the Xoom 160 will return 40kmpl, realistically one should expect 35kmpl when ridden sanely and around 32-33kmpl while going gung ho.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:
## IS IT COMFY?

Don’t be too bothered by the 142kg weight figure as Hero has found a great way to mask its heft. The Xoom 160 is very well balanced with the mass cleverly optimised for you to not be super bothered by it. Moving it around in the parking is also not a pain and propping it on the main stand takes little effort.

One cannot miss the spine and getting used to the lack of storage space on the floor wouldn’t take much time. What will take some getting used to is that you will have to sprawl your legs slightly wider than usual at traffic stops as the floor is particularly wide. The seat remains fairly accommodating enough so that even shorter riders find their footing rather easily.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 7)
page_chunks.content:
## IS IT COMFY?

My grouse with the posture arises from the way the spine has been designed as it isn’t straight. It has an angle that makes gripping it an issue during sport riding. And in case you do decide to extend your feet forwards and go into a relaxed touring-friendly posture, your feet stick out dramatically. With my large size 10 boots, almost all of my toes were exposed and not protected in any manner by the body.

Another particular niggle with the Xoom 160 is the soft padding. This is a typical trait of Hero’s products and it starts to bug the rider on long tours. Urban hustling will not be a bother, though.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## DOES IT SOAK BUMPS WELL?

Plush ride? Naah. The Xoom 160 offers a balanced and neutral ride with a taut suspension tune. Hence, on bad roads and small undulations, the imperfections filter through without causing a lot of discomfort. The rear shocks are particularly bouncy and take a while to regain composure. This feeling is a lot more controlled when riding with a pillion as the suspension is tuned for a two-up riding experience. If you're going to be riding solo, take it with a little bit of caution. It is definitely a tad bit on the sportier side, but not jarring and not painful like the original Aerox.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## IS IT SPORTY?

The Xoom handles city traffic with ease, lane changes requiring a little effort but nothing too demanding. Around long sweepers it holds its own well and is fun in its own right. Just don’t expect it to be sharp and nimble in the twisties cause then it will start to falter.

Now, one thing to absolutely note is that the MRF Kurve block-pattern tyres are not the grippiest. These fail to instill any amount of confidence and break traction almost too soon when it starts to rain. Grippier alternatives from Reise Moto would have made the experience all the more confidence inspiring.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## DOES IT OFFER MAX CONVENIENCE?

Given the maxi styling, one would expect a large underseat storage space. However, it is far from being called generous or humungous. You do get the option of remote boot unlock, which is convenient, but the actual space is not more than most of its rivals. At 22-litres, it can just about gobble up an ISI-certified full face helmet. However, a proper internationally-certified one doesn’t fit rather well. Hero will sell you a top box of either 22-litres or 29-litres, with the latter likely to be capable of storing your helmet.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## IS IT FEATURE-LOADED?

The main thing that still bugs me about Hero’s premium products is the fact that the feature list isn’t as impressive as its commuters. Keyless ignition and a smart key are good bits to have. But the switchgear: felt relevant for the 2010s, not 2025. In fact, the new Hero Glamour X 125 that was recently launched and costs nearly half a lakh rupees less, has better switches.

And let’s just not talk about the dated LCD console. It is rather boring, plain jane and has no business being on a scooter of its ilk in 2025. Yes, it has bluetooth integration with turn-by-turn navigation but it feels out of place on the Xoom. Perhaps a future variant with the same colour TFT screen from the Hero XPulse 210 would serve the premium proposition of the scooter well.

page_chunks.title: Hero Xoom 160 Maxi-Scooter First Ride Review And Impressions: Engine, Price, Handling, Comfort, Features, Verdict, Rivals, Performance, Ride Quality, And More  - ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## WORTH THE WAIT?

Absolutely. The Xoom 160 meets India’s growing aspirations and is a great step-up from a 125cc scooter. It is just as competent in the city as it is on the highway. It delights you when you roll on the throttle and stays composed when taking on long sweeping bends. What we ideally would have wanted is for Hero to update the feature set on this maxi- scooter. The screen should not belong on a scooter such as this. And while it is at it, maybe some better tyres also.

At Rs 1,48,500 (ex-showroom, Delhi), this Hero scooter is definitely worth your consideration. And the brand surely would like to pass on the new GST slab benefits on to the buyers, so expect the asking price to go lower as well.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World  - ZigWheels (part 1)
page_chunks.content:
## Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World

- Published September 8, 2025
- Views : 8386
- 5 min read

We recently had a chance to experience a wide range of Eurogrip’s new tyres as part of the Eurogrip TreadTalks. We had a chance to visit the brand’s factory in Madurai and then head for a 200km ride to Kodaikanal, through some of the most scenic routes in South India. After testing out 3 different tyres during the course of this event, here’s what our experience was like.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## The Factory & The Bikes

We first visited the brand’s factory and got a glimpse at how Eurogrip makes its tyres. We saw everything from how the compounds are mixed to how the final tyres are treaded. This experience really gave us an insight into how every small thing, from the compounds used to the thread pattern, comes together to create the perfect tyre.

After that, we were introduced to the bikes, and there were a plethora of models to choose from. Over the course of this experience, I had a chance to ride 3 bikes extensively, the Royal Enfield Classic 350, the Yamaha MT-15 and the Yamaha R15.

As an MT-15 owner, I really wanted to test out the bike because it would be easier for me to judge the difference in handling. Aside from this, I have also been looking to put new tyres on my bike, so this was a good chance to see if the tyres offered by Eurogrip would be a good choice. Before moving on to the experience, here’s a breakdown of the tyres that were offered with each bike:

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## The Factory & The Bikes

| **Model** | **Front Size & Tyre** | **Rear Size & Tyre** |
| Royal Enfield Classic 350 | 90/90-19 Terrabite DB+ | 120/80-18 Terrabite DB+ |
| Yamaha MT-15 | 100/80-17 Beamer HS+ | 140/70 R17 Protorq Extreme |
| Yamaha R15 | 110/70 R17 Protorq Extreme | 140/70 R17 Protorq Extreme |

Out of these 3 different models, one of them just blew me away with its amazing performance and the massive difference made in terms of handling, and here’s the story.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## Classic 350 & Terrabite DB+

For the first leg of our journey, I got the Royal Enfield Classic 350. The bike was a good choice, as the early stages involved around 50 kilometres of highway riding.

During this time, the tyres inspired a lot of confidence and kept the bike stable at highway speeds of 80kmph. Even when pushed hard, up to 100 kmph, there was no issue with grip and the bike was very stable. After covering the highways, we got to the twisty mountain roads, and here things changed.

The Terrabite’s excellent grip gave me a lot of confidence to lean in the twisties. But it became clear that the Classic 350 doesn’t have enough cornering ground clearance, so I scraped the footpegs throughout the ride. I eventually had to be a bit less aggressive with the lean and ride at a slightly slower pace.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
## Classic 350 & Terrabite DB+

Another thing which prompted this change of pace was loose gravel and wet patches of roads, which were present mid-corners in some of the sections. The tyres held up well in the wet sections, so wet grip in general was not a particular cause of concern. But I personally didn’t want to take any chances, especially with the loose gravel. The experience overall was quite exciting, and with the Terrabite DB+ tyres, proved that even roadsters like the Classic 350 can be fun in the twisties.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:
## Yamaha MT-15 & The Beamer HS+

After a while in the twisties, we took a break, and I used this opportunity to change bikes. I got the Yamaha MT-15, and my colleague who owns a Dominar 400, swapped his Gixxer for the Dominar 400. During the second leg of the journey, we got to experience our own bikes in a different way.

The Yamaha MT-15 felt really different, and the addition of the softer compound Protorq at the rear inspired a lot of confidence, with much better feel than the stock tyres. The Beamer HS+ tyre is meant mostly for city commutes, so the choice felt a bit odd as we were mostly riding in the twisties. The front tyre did hold up pretty well under hard braking, but overall, it didn’t offer the kind of confidence you’d hope for in the twisties. Overall, the MT-15 was quite enjoyable with these tyres and felt much better than the stock ones.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World  - ZigWheels (part 7)
page_chunks.content:
## Yamaha R15 And Protorq Extremes

During our return to Madurai, I took the Yamaha R15, which got Protorq Extremes at both ends. Now, out of the experience so far, this has to be the biggest highlight and the section where I had the most fun.

I first had a chance to **try out the tyres on the Aprilia Tuono 457** back when I had reviewed the motorcycle. During that time, the Protorq Extremes were a major plus point of the motorcycle and made the experience all the more enjoyable. I also got to briefly try them out on the Dominar 400 that my colleague was riding, so I had a lot of expectations. When I got the R15 and started riding, the tyres didn’t leave me disappointed and exceeded my expectations.

page_chunks.title: Eurogrip TreadTalks: Experiencing 3 Different Tyre Series In The Real World  - ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## Yamaha R15 And Protorq Extremes

I was able to lean the bike with ease, and there was no fear of a lack of grip. When we returned to Madurai, we were greeted with a heavy downpour, and the roads were quite wet for a considerable distance. Even on these wet roads, I didn’t feel like I needed to slow down or cut down my pace overall. When the roads got dry, the experience became even better, and if I were looking for sporty tyres today for the best performance on my bike, then the Protorqs will be my go-to. That said, I will tell you a whole lot more about this if I get my hands on them.

page_chunks.content:
## Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level

- Published August 18, 2025
- Views : 8706
- 6 min read

At first, it’s easy to think of the Volvo EX30 as a car similar to the EX40 (formally known as the XC40 Recharge) but smaller. However, it doesn’t take long to see there’s a lot that’s new here. There are portions that will intrigue and annoy at the same time, but the end result is certainly an experience with a difference.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 2)
page_chunks.content:
## Looks

The shape is unusual. It’s somehow boxy and curvy at the same time. Its styling stands out easily but that’s especially true if you were to get it in a brighter colour. In fact, we got to see it in a bright shade of yellow that, oddly, Volvo India teased us with but isn’t offering here in India. Instead, you have the corporate-friendly collection of white, grey, beige, black and a sky blue - pretty but they don’t unlock the shock-and-awe this design is capable of.

The Thor’s Hammer DRLs are now grid-patterned, the tail lights fit into the rear end like a brace and the 19-inch wheels get a piano black finish at the centre that, from some angles, make the outer metallic-finish edges look like they’re floating.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 3)
page_chunks.content:
## Looks

There are some odd quirks too. The wing mirrors are fully-movable i.e. the mirrors don’t adjust independently from the mirror covers. And the button to open the powered tailgate is hidden so well (it’s just above the ‘L’ in the rear badging) that mall security will likely look like a mime as they try and feel for where the button may be.

Also, there’s no physical key. You use an NFC key-card or a phone-integrated digital key. While these are convenient, there are limitations. No key means valets have nothing to tie your car’s details to when you pop-over to your choicest 5-star hotel (it does come with a case if you’d like). And the NFC key card only works on the driver’s door.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 4)
page_chunks.content:
## Boot Space

The car on our drive didn’t have the space-saver spare tyre that Volvo says customer cars will get. At 318-400 litres (measured to the backrest-roof), there’s enough space for 3-4 cabin-sized trolley bags and some backpacks or one large suitcase. The boot floor level is adjustable too and the seats do split and fold ahead. Of course, if Volvo plonks a big spare tyre atop the boot floor, the space is rendered more or less inconsequential, save for some small bags.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 5)
page_chunks.content:
## Cabin Space & Quality

I don’t expect anyone to buy the EX30 for its back seat. The front seats are comfortable enough, even for those of a heavier build and who stretch around or above 6ft in height. Sure, there’s space for average-sized adults in the rear but the under thigh support here is weak. No rear AC vents either and in Jaipur’s sweltering heat, this did prove to be a challenge. The fixed panoramic glass roof is, of course, heat-insulated but there’s no sunshade. Aside from the obvious visual sun exposure it’s also an opportunity for pigeons to run a Rorschach test on you. Volvo does offer a manually-installed foldable sunshade as an accessory overseas but a powered sunshade would’ve just made so much more sense.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 6)
page_chunks.content:
## Cabin Space & Quality

The interior quality is good but not in your typical German car manner where you have several metallic or wood-like inserts to give you premium touch points. Instead, you get a blend of recycled/recyclable materials that aren’t usual to the touch. There’s an insert in the dashboard and the door pads that almost has a granite like touch and feel to it. And the design itself is Tesla-like in its minimalist approach.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 7)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

The EX30’s power window controls (front and rear) and door locks are centre console-integrated and there’s nothing on the doors. Even the powered front seats have a single squared-dial that controls all the functions including lumbar-adjustment (lumbar-adjustment on the driver’s seat only).

There’s no instrument cluster - just a steering-column mounted scanner that monitors the driver’s movements for attention-assist. Everything else in the car is managed through the 12.3-touchscreen, including the dual-zone climate control, mirror and light settings. Even the gear selector and speedometer are on this central screen only.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 8)
page_chunks.content:
## Features

The touchscreen comes with Google Maps, YouTube and the PlayStore on board so Android Auto isn’t offered separately. But you do have Apple CarPlay as well. Interestingly the front doors don’t have speakers with a large sound-bar integrated near the front windshield instead - part of the 9-speaker Harman Kardon sound system which offers good sound quality.

Aside from the wireless phone charger, there are type-C chargers in the front and rear.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 9)
page_chunks.content:
## Safety

Unsurprisingly, the EX30 gets a 5-star Euro NCAP crash safety rating.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 10)
page_chunks.content:
## Safety Features

| Blind-Spot Warning | 360-degree Camera |
| Dual front, side, curtain and front central airbag | Auto-emergency braking |
| Adaptive Cruise Control | Tyre Pressure Display |
| Lane-assist and lane-departure warning | Front & Rear Cross-Traffic Alert and Auto-Brake |
| Auto Headlights | Rain-Sensing Wipers |

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 11)
page_chunks.content:
## Storage

There are some notable quirks to the storage spaces. The front central storage has adjustable flaps and the central storage console runs right through to the rear. Rear passengers get a removable tray here too. The glovebox opens via the touchscreen only and is located in the middle instead of on the front passenger’s side. And even the cupholders are hidden away under the front armrest in a solid pop-out tray. We didn’t think storage spaces could be a conversation piece but in the EX30, they are!

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 12)
page_chunks.content:
## Drive And Ride Quality

In India, the EX30 is offered with rear-wheel drive only with a motor good for 272PS/343Nm. That’s enough to get it from 0-100kmph in 5.3 seconds. The 69kWh battery pack (NMC) has a WLTP-rated range of 480km, so 400-450km in the real world isn’t far-fetched to expect.

The EX30 is quick and calm and there’s no witchcraft needed to unlock the Jekyll and Hyde within. No range of drive modes to choose from and regenerative braking’s limited to the one-pedal mode too. This can be an exciting car because of how it can accelerate but it’s equally enjoyable to drive peacefully within city confines.

The ride quality is notably on the firmer side but not jarringly so. It’s typical German car fare but while the design may say SUV, the experience in terms of high speed stability, ride quality and ground clearance is closer to a sedan.

page_chunks.title: Volvo EX30 Review: A Different Kind Of Entry-Level  - ZigWheels (part 13)
page_chunks.content:
## Verdict

Entry-level luxury cars are often a hard sell because their value-propositions are rarely strong enough to justify the price. The EX30 is assembled in India itself with prices expected in September 2025 and deliveries a month later. We expect a price of around Rs 42-44 lakh (ex-showroom) at which price it makes for a great self-driven compact luxury car that’s quick, quirky and quite Swedish in how it makes you feel special.

## What is an MUV car?

An MUV (Multi Utility Vehicle) or an MPV (Multi Purpose Vehicle) is a van-shaped vehicle that can be used to ferry passengers and cargo as it offers plenty of storage and seating space. An MUV can seat up to 9 passengers.

## What is the difference between SUV and MUV?

SUV stands for Sport Utility Vehicle while MUV or MPV stands for Multi Utility Vehicle or Multi Purpose Vehicle. While most SUVs are oriented for off-roading, an MUV/MPV is more of a van suited for large families and hauling cargo.

## About BMW

**History**

German automaker BMW has a legacy of building driver-centric luxury cars with cutting-edge technology. It began operations over a century ago as an aircraft engine manufacturer, and has been producing cars since the 1930s.

As a carmaker, BMW landed in India in 2006, and had a new plant in Chennai by 2007. The 5 Series and 3 Series luxury sedans were its first cars, and later in 2012, it introduced the Mini brand in the country. It has been able to keep car prices in check with local assembly, but new fully imported electric vehicles attract a premium.

**Product portfolio**

Luxury Sedans: BMW offers the 3 Series, 5 Series and 7 Series sedans, and the 2 Series, 6 Series and 8 Series Gran Coupes in India. The 3 Series is also available as a long-wheelbase Gran Limousine and a sportier M340i sedan. In addition, BMW offers the Z4 and Z4 M40i two-door roadster, and the M2 Competition, M5 Competition, M760Li, and M8 performance sedans.

Coupe SUVs: Two coupe SUVs are part of the carmaker’s lineup in India – the BMW X4 and X6.

Electric vehicles: BMW’s EV lineup consists of the iX electric SUV.

## ORA Cars

China’s Great Wall Motors (GWM) has officially introduced its new brand dedicated exclusively to new energy vehicles. ORA is the fourth brand under the carmaker’s roof after Great Wall, Haval and WEY and will aim their EVs at young audiences with the first model due this year.Great Wall label ORA, or Ola in Chinese, had been announced some weeks ago but has now revealed details at the official launch at the Beijing Motor Show.Their first electric cars are both planned out already. The ORA iQ5 is a sedan with a said range of 350 km and a motor output of 60hp, good for a 150kph max. Next one up in 2019 is the ORA R1, a more compact EV with a rather urban range of 300 km.The two models stand for two lines ORA is to introduce, the iQ line with electric cars of regular size, and the R line with small city cars. They will be sold through a separate dealer network.Great Wall also says that all the ORA models will sit on dedicated and unique EV platforms.

## Mahindra XUV 3XO ZNG – A CNG SUV Without Usual Compromise

- Mahindra has launched the XUV 3XO ZNG in four manual-only CNG variants, its first CNG model.
- Its 1.2-litre turbo-petrol engine keeps the same output on CNG (about 110 bhp and 200 Nm), but twin cylinder setup under the boot floor eats into luggage space.
- It suits high mileage buyers who want lower running costs without losing performance, though lack of an automatic and reduced boot space.

## XUV 3XO Pros and Cons

**Good Things**

- Spacious cabin with enough legroom, headroom, and cabin width for 5 occupants
- Petrol and diesel engine options offer a strong balance of refinement and performance
- Loaded with features: Panoramic sunroof, digital instrument cluster, 2-zone climate control, and a Harman Kardon music system, 6 airbags, ABS with EBD, ISOFIX as standard
- Higher variants add 360-degree camera and front parking sensors too
- Advanced driver assistance features such as lane-assist and adaptive cruise control are well-tuned for Indian driving conditions
- Good ride comfort and high speed stability even with passengers and luggage on board

**Could be Better**

- Rivals like the Kia Sonet and Tata Nexon offer more boot space
- Missing features: Ventilated seats, powered driver’s seat, ambient lighting, parcel tray
- Turbo-petrol engine’s fuel-efficiency especially in heavy traffic will be low (10-12 kmpl)

**Expert's Conclusion**
